#3540. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3539. Jennifer Lopez 'Cried for 6 Months' Amid Kids Leaving for College

Jennifer Lopez is opening up about life as an empty nester after her 18-year-old twins, Max and Emme, started college this past fall.

“They went to college. It’s crazy. I still have on my phone [a photo of] them on my lap as babies. It goes so fast, just like everybody says,” Lopez, 57, shared on the Sunday, November 15, episode of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.

The Office Romance actress said that she was incredibly emotional from the time her children — whom she shares with ex-husband Marc Anthony — graduated from high school right through to their departures for college.

“It’s all the feelings. It’s one of those moments in life where you’re just like, you’re sad, you’re melancholy, but you’re excited and you’re hopeful. There’s so many feelings that go with it,” Lopez explained. “I cried for six months straight [from] two months before they graduated [high school] until I dropped them off [at college] and a few weeks after that. You’re gonna die. It’s definitely a thing.”

Despite missing her children, Lopez shared that she is feeling a sense of freedom now that her children are college age, describing herself as being in a “happy era.”

She said, “[It’s] the first time since I was like, in my early 20s, that I haven’t been with someone, had my kids. I’m alone. I’m free. I can do whatever the f*** I want. It’s kind of amazing but also weird.

The multihypenate star is now back in the studio recording new music and embracing her newfound freedom. (One of Lopez’s new tracks is inspired by her kids leaving for college, she revealed in October.)

“When the kids were leaving, I was having so many feelings and so many emotions that I went into the studio and started kind of playing around and making music, and now I’ve made 20 songs,” she said. “I feel like I’m only halfway done. I need to be in there longer.”

She added, “This does feel like a happy era where I feel unencumbered with anything kind of unhealthy. It’s just a very healthy time of my life. I’m on my own. I feel like it’s another coming of age that happens in our lives. I think a lot of parents will relate to that.”

Back in May, Lopez said she had been “crying for two months” as her children prepared to graduate from high school.

“It’s fine. I want them to be happy, go where they want to go, and do what they want to do,” the proud mama shared on Jimmy Kimmel Live! at the time.

“I remember being that age and thinking I couldn’t wait to get out in the world and do my thing. I really wanted to get out,” she said. “All year people have been asking me, ‘Oh, they’re going away to college, is it going to be terrible?’ No, it’s going to be great. I want them to go out there. I want them to do what they want to do. They have big dreams. They have things they want to do. It’s going to be great.”

The Damon/Kimmel faux feud has been going on for decades at this point, and it just never gets old. Matt Damon and Jimmy Kimmel have been pretending to hate each other for years, doing bits about it at the Oscars and on Kimmel’s talk show. And despite actually being great friends, they love to keep this bit going. On that note, the talk show host was recently asked to give a toast to Matt Damon at a huge Hollywood event, and there's a hilarious video that I just can't get enough of!

Damon has had quite a year, having released The Rip, which co-stars his best friend, Ben Affleck. The Rip was also a huge hit for Netflix and allowed for him to continue to work with Affleck amid other projects at their production company. Damon was also most notably the star of The Odyssey, which grossed well over a billion dollars worldwide and is an awards season favorite. As a result, GQ named Damon one of their Men of the Year in their annual issue. At the party to celebrate the magazine. Jimmy Kimmel gave quite the speech, which you can see below:

Kimmel, of course, couldn’t resist mentioning some controversial people named in GQ magazine over the years to compare Damon, too. On top of that, the talk show was quick to say that Tom Holland was more deserving of this honor. Kimmel said:

Matt had a big year and he's in great company. I've made a list of some of the other honorees. Mel Gibson, 1996, 2007, Kanye West. The list goes on and on and you you deserve it. You really do. Not as much as others might deserve it. You know, Tom Holland was in the Odyssey and Spider-Man this year. He was in number one and number two. You're just number two. You're a big number two. You deserve this.

Kimmel then toasted to his faux foe and fittingly called him “Mrs. Ben Affleck.” Of course, Damon had his own hilarious quips as a response. He was quick to point out one key detail about that night, saying:

I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place.

Of course, this is all in good fun, and the riffing is expected any time these two guys are in the same room together. It started back in the early 2000s when Jimmy Kimmel started saying “Apologies to Matt Damon, we ran out of time” at the end of every show. It was a self-deprecating joke, as a way to make fun of how terrible his guests were when his show first started, as opposed to having a movie star like Damon. It became a running joke that continued even as Kimmel’s show became more successful.

Periodically, Damon tries to sneak onto Kimmel’s show, and the host jokingly refuses to have the actor on as a guest. They also make fun of each other relentlessly in public, and hilariously compete for the affection of Ben Affleck. It’s a great bit, and if this GQ speech is any indication, this duo isn’t planning on retiring the quips anytime soon. I hope they continue to dig at each other for years to come, because it is just too much fun to watch.

Fans can check out Matt Damon in The Odyssey, which is still playing in select theaters nationwide. It’s the tail end of The Odyssey’s historic box office run, so make sure to see it on the big screen while you still can. You can also watch Jimmy Kimmel Live!, which airs at 11:35 p.m. ET on ABC and is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription.

#3537. Andrew Scott On What Makes Elsinore “So Moving”

Although the emotional core of Elsinore is centered around beloved actor Ian Charleston dealing with terminal illness, its star Andrew Scott says the film has as much heart as it does humor.

“The most singular thing about our film I think is the humor in it,” he said during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “The tragedy in some ways is a little bit like Hamlet itself, but you can't make a film about Ian Charleston without having gags in it. He was incredibly funny. Every person [who knew him] said he was just wickedly funny, and flirtatious, and he was always looking towards the light, and he had a certain degree of courage. So that is something I think that we all share as a sense of humor.”

Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, Stephen Beresford and Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Elsinore tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Scott has received early acclaim for his powerful portrayal of Charleson. Before the film began Vanity Fair’s West Coast Editor John Ross warned the audience that "first you're going to laugh, then you're going to cry," while watching Scott’s performance.

“I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” continued Scott. “So that to me was the thing that we were the most

insistent on in some ways. And that's really all down to finding actors who in this extraordinary ensemble have a really terrific sense of humor. And we kind of knew that we could, with the screenplay, get the best actors in the country. And I feel we did.”

The panel conversation featured Scott, costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford, following an exclusive screening of the film.

Billie Piper at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Piper, who plays Charleston's close friend Patsy, she relied heavily on Beresford's script for her prep, as well as information she gleaned from those who actually knew Patsy, and Charleston.

“I've spoken to a few members of the family, their friends, and then I sort of cherry-picked things from people I'd known in the beginning of my career, the louder figures in our industry,” she said. “And then I did my own interpretation and just had a good time. It's a very moving story, but I had a lot of fun playing that part. She's a really joyful character to play, I enjoyed the comedy. And I understand that a lot of her jokes are coming from a place of despair.”

Beresford, who has known Scott for 25 years, said he didn't initially think of his longtime friend for the role, but should have.

“The story of Ian, and Ian's Hamlet [performance] is legendary in the British theater,” he said. “So many people said it was the greatest Hamlet they'd ever seen, and that it had this incredible quality. So I knew about the story, and then it was brought to me actually as an idea by a producer who said, ‘What about writing about Ian Charleston, and what about Andrew playing Ian Charleston?’ And then I just thought, ‘Well, why didn't I have that idea myself five years ago?’ So yeah, that's really how it happened, and I started to research it, the details of the story were so incredible, and so moving.”

Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

Scott, who famously played Hamlet onstage 150 times beginning in 2017, prior to filming Elsinore, closed out the panel conversation by reciting his favorite line from the classic tragedy.

“When Hamlet says the line about the war that was going on—and this was written 400 years ago—it just seems so relevant to what he might have been experiencing at the time, which is: ‘I see the imminent death of 20,000 men who for a fantasy, a trick of fame, go to their graves like beds.’ The idea that that was written 400 years ago, and that he was watching 50 percent of his friends die for no reason and be neglected by governments, and derided by the public. And it was just happening, and happening time and time again.”

Scott continued: “The reason that I love it so much is that when I was doing Hamlet myself, of course I wasn't thinking about the AIDS crisis, but the enduring nature of art, something that was written 400 years ago by Shakespeare, could actually be of use to somebody in 1989 and then be reproduced again in 2026 and be of use. And that idea of art being useful down the lines is so moving to me.”

Vanity Fair's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, Elsinore stars Andrew Scott and Billie Piper and writer Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

#3536. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3535. Patrick Stewart Had A Small But Important Role In One Of The Best Animated Movies Of The '90s

It feels impossible to do justice to the late Sir Patrick Stewart with mere words, but we can attempt it. One part of his incredible legacy is voice acting; how could he not try his hand there when he had such a magnificent voice? Stewart's defining voice role is probably the eccentric CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on "American Dad." Casting him against type there is the whole joke. Patrick Stewart, famous for playing dignified, fatherly authority figures like Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, is the one saying all of Bullock's ridiculous, profane, and unhinged lines, which become even funnier read in his baritone voice.

The folks behind the biblical epic "The Prince of Egypt" also knew the weight Stewart's voice carried. At Steven Spielberg's suggestion, DreamWorks Animation adapted the first stretch of the Book of Exodus, or how the prophet Moses (Val Kilmer) — raised as an Egyptian prince — discovered his true heritage and led his people out of bondage. Patrick Stewart plays Pharaoh Seti, adoptive father of Moses and the man who ordered the massacre of Hebrew babies that made Moses' mother send him away. Stewart/Seti has only a few scant scenes in the movie's first act, but he casts a shadow as wide as any pyramid over the rest of the film.

As with later DreamWorks pictures, "The Prince of Egypt" employs celebrity voice casting: Kilmer as Moses, Ralph Fiennes as Moses' brother/Seti's son Pharaoh Rameses, etc. But here, it mostly works — mostly. Jeff Goldblum as Moses' brother Aaron is a distracting bit of casting where you hear the actor first, not the character. "Prince of Egypt" doesn't disguise Stewart's voice either (you probably couldn't with a voice of such power), but it complements his character to a chilling effect.

In "The Prince of Egypt," Seti first appears admonishing his two sons for being reckless in a chariot race. He's especially harsh on his heir, Rameses, explaining that "one weak link can break the chain of a mighty dynasty." When Moses asks his father to go easier on Rameses, Seti offers understanding (and pure dramatic irony): "Moses, you will never have to carry a burden like the crown I will pass to Rameses."

Pretty typical Patrick Stewart, right? Seti is stern but reasonable, some of the same qualities that made Captain Picard such a respected leader. His respect-commanding voice is even more effective as a disappointed father, too; would you want to hear "I'm disappointed in you" from that voice?

But then Moses learns the truth about where he came from, and how. Seeing his son in despair, Seti is gentle but also doesn't deny he had a generation of Hebrew babies murdered as population control. The animation and Stewart's performance work in perfect sync. In Seti's whispered tone, he sounds genuinely pained. Even if his claim "sometimes, for the greater good, sacrifices must be made," rings hollow here, Seti's thousand yard stare tells us that maybe he does feel the weight of what he did and realizes he's damned for it.

But then the kicker comes: He tries to "comfort" Moses that the babies cast into the Nile "were only slaves." The dissonance of Seti loving his own family and also being a genocidal enslaver is potent, but sadly believable. Fittingly, this is also the last time we see him in the film, because the bond he shared with Moses has been severed.

"The Prince of Egypt" is one of the most gorgeously animated films ever made, and it's not only the animation that's beautifully crafted. The storytelling is sharp and mature. It sits at the very fine line of being simple enough for kids and complex enough for adults; Moses and Rameses being turned from beloved brothers to enemies by forces much bigger than themselves is painful to watch.

Right off, "The Prince of Egypt" is an unconventional title for the Exodus story; after all, the whole story is about Moses rejecting that life for his people by birth. (Compare it to the 1956 biblical epic titled "The Ten Commandments.") But the movie paints Moses' deliverance of his people as bittersweet, since it cost him the brother he loved.

Though not nearly as controversial as Nikos Kazantzakis's book (and later Martin Scorsese's film) "The Last Temptation of Christ," "The Prince of Egypt" similarly invents human drama from scripture. "Last Temptation" works from the tenet that Jesus was both fully divine but also fully human. So, then, wouldn't he be afflicted by man's foibles and doubts? The Book of Exodus holds that Moses was raised as an Egyptian in the Pharaoh's own family. Wouldn't Moses, then, feel pained about having to turn his back on the home where he was raised, even if he recognized the necessity of God's plan for him?

Part of the tragedy is that this only flows one way. After Moses learns the truth, he can't look at the enslaved Hebrew workers without thinking their birthright is also his. Conversely, neither Seti nor Rameses clock that the son/brother they love would've been just another of those slaves. It's an excellent use of Patrick Stewart, twisting our relationship to his fatherly presence and providing an undercurrent of darkness to it.

#3534. Hillary Clinton Showed Up For Dinner at Gloria Steinem’s Townhouse

It’s a dark and stormy November night at Gloria Steinem’s townhouse, and Hillary Clinton has something to say about the 2026 election. “One of my most anticipated moments will be watching Donald Trump walk into the State of the Union through the now more than one hundred women members of the House of Representatives. I just want them all to stare at him and say, ‘You fired us from jobs we were qualified for. You insulted us. You demeaned our ambition. You undermined our place in government and society. And we’re here.’”

Huma Abedin, Busy Philips, and Paloma Elsesser.

The former Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate is a last-minute but highly anticipated arrival to this dinner honoring Steinem, the late activist. She passed away in September, but the feminist pathfinder was known for throwing these salon-type events (she called them “circles”) at her Upper East Side townhouse, which she bought for just $30,000 in the late ’60s. It’s overflowing with books (I spy Marilyn by Norman Mailer, Jane Fonda’s War by Mary Hershberger, and several Eleanor Roosevelt biographies on the shelves), pictures (there’s one framed of Steinem alongside Mariska Hargitay) and Indian art. (Steinem spent two formative years in the country.) There are magnets in her kitchen of Wonder Woman, Frida Kahlo, and a cloth finger puppet of Hillary Clinton. A political button is pinned to it that says “Another Bitch for Hillary.” The whole place smells like a Cire Trudon candle, and everyone’s drinking negronis. (Which actually isn’t technically very Steinem—her favorite cocktail was a margarita—but the negronis go with the night’s dinner, prepared by Lilia chef Missy Robbins.) Yet this is one of the first events at the townhouse that Steinem herself isn’t here to lead.

Jihae, Lux Pascal, Naomi Watts, and Bethann Hardison.

Amy Richards, a feminist activist whom many consider to be the daughter Steinem never had—a title Richards rejects because her mentor “didn’t want kids”—stood up at one point to tell the crowd that this is what Steinem would have wanted. Growing up with a transient father and a mentally volatile mother, the late activist took near-obsessive care in maintaining a welcoming home she could share with others. “As long as I knew Gloria, she always said, ‘I just want my home to be the way it’s always been.’ She wanted it to be filled with people,” Richards says. “She didn’t grow up with a home. She was traveling the country for the first 10 years of her life and then lived with her mother, who was not very stable.”

At least Steinem’s still here on the wall: Months before her death, she posed for a series of portraits by Paola Kudacki for Weldun, a platform that offers physically adaptive and functional fashion. It was a bit of a small miracle that Steinem said yes. “I will say, Gloria did not always love to be photographed,” Richards says. “Especially in her later years—not because of wrinkles or aging, but she was just like, ‘Aren’t there enough pictures of me?’” Weldun and the Gloria Steinem Foundation are presenting tonight’s dinner, and mementos of Steinem are everywhere. On the fireplace mantle sits a pair of her signature Ray-Ban aviators. But Gloria’s stuff isn’t the same as Gloria herself.

Former secretary of state Hillary Clinton hugging Melissa McCarthy.

Which is probably why, in a crowd of women that include Huma Abedin, Mariska Hargitay, Padma Lakshmi, Melissa McCarthy, and Bethann Hardison—who, at the ripe age of 84, shows up wearing Gucci—Clinton’s unexpected arrival feels seismic, like Gloria sent someone in her place. (Hardison tells me she thinks Steinem used whatever divine power she’s got up there to launch the Blue Wave: “She’s probably saying she helped it happen!”) Whatever your views on Clinton’s politics, she was the first woman to receive a presidential nomination from a major party. Paloma Elsesser and I sit crouched in a corner of the room, glued to the window. “There’s mother,” the supermodel whispers to me as Clinton exits her car into the pouring rain and walks up to the townhouse door.

Guests at dinner honoring the late Gloria Steinem.

“Hi, everybody,” Clinton says as she walks in. The entire dinner comes to a silent halt. “Hi,” the room responds in unison. Madame Secretary doesn’t seem to like the fuss, probably because 30 or so people intensely staring at you when you arrive at a party is objectively unsettling. “Go back to eating!” she says, motioning to the Missy Robbins meal on the table. Clinton sits down next to Naomi Watts and warmly greets Busy Philips, who stumped for Clinton back in 2016. Hargitay blows her a kiss across the table. All anyone wants to do is talk to Clinton about the 2026 election, in which Democrats won at least 55 seats in the Senate and 256 in the House to take both majorities in the US Congress. At the end of the meal—and after a proper catch-up with Shonda Rhimes—Clinton tries to leave, but she can’t. Guests block the door, clamoring to chat her up.

Amid the Clinton traffic jam, I ask Hargitay about the photo. She can’t remember exactly what it is from. “Was it Bravo? Was it with Andy…what’s his name?” But she can guess what she thinks Steinem might say about the blue wave: “There is a God!”

I watch Clinton finally make her exit. It’s late, so I wait several minutes before I descend the stairs to leave too. (I wait for Elsesser, Watts, Hardinn, and Lux Pascal to finish taking a selfie on the steps.) But I spoke too soon: Clinton’s stuck waiting for the coat check, another group of women crowded around her hoping to say something—or, more likely, hoping she says something. With the way this night is going, Clinton might be the last one at the party.

#3533. I Ain't Got No Body: The Various Non-Corporeal Aliens In Star Trek Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

One of the primary features of "Star Trek" is theoretical biology. Given the wide panoply of alien species on display throughout the franchise, audiences have been invited to ponder alternate evolutionary paths besides the one that happened to bring us into being on Earth. What kind of planetary conditions would be required to form, say, a hyper-intelligent crystalline being? How did a horta evolve? What will we evolve into in the future? Will our brains adapt to become psychic over time? According to the "Star Trek: Voyager" episode "Threshold" (one of the show's most outraging to fans), it was revealed that humans will eventually evolve into giant salamanders.

This leads to a few logical evolutionary extremes, like the fact that some species on "Star Trek" have evolved into beings of pure energy. "Star Trek" has many examples of non-corporeal aliens who can only be perceived as light, as a psychic presence, as a sound, or as a vision beamed directly into our inferior, corporeal brains. To cite a notable example: In the original series episode "Is There In Truth No Beauty?," audiences were introduced to the Medusans, a highly intelligent, telepathic, and empathic species whose light-constructed bodies are so wildly complex that any human looking at them would instantly go mad. Only a mentally disciplined species like the Vulcans could look at a Medusan, and even then required a special filtered visor (pictured above).

These kinds of aliens expand the audience's mind as to what can be considered life.

In looking at fictional non-corporeal species, "Star Trek" expands our horizons. We're invited to ponder new perspectives about basic concepts like evolution, time, the nature of consciousness, and, perhaps, our own relationship to the cosmos. Non-corporeal entities are one of the coolest ideas "Star Trek" has to offer, and their recurring nature is a constant reminder that life is more complex, and the cosmos more ineffable, than we could ever hope to imagine.

On "Star Trek," non-corporeal aliens tend to appear as lights or clouds or glowing mists of energy. One might recall the smoke-like alien that made Kirk nervous in the episode "Obsession," one of the more underrated episodes of the show. Others might immediately think of Zefram Cochrane's glowing, cloud-like "companion" in the episode "Metamorphosis." That entity had the ability to sort of intuitively communicate with Cochrane (Glenn Corbett), and could also heal diseases and sustain human life beyond its usual biological barriers. A common theme of non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek" is that they are godlike and powerful, able to tap into the powers of the universe in ways we don't understand.

The Medusans may be one of the most popular non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek," but fans of "Deep Space Nine" would surely want me to acknowledge the wormhole aliens, a.k.a. The Prophets. In that show's pilot episode, "Emissary," Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) travels into a stable wormhole and encounters bodiless creatures who can only communicate with him by appearing as people from his memories.

The wormhole aliens from "Deep Space Nine" are so, well, alien, they don't understand concepts like linguistic communication or linear time. They don't see cause leading to effect, but rather a widespread series of events that happen all at once. Sisko has to do the impossible, and explain the human habit of seeing time as a straight line.

And, of course, there are many species of godlike beings on "Star Trek" who often take the form of humans, despite not having physical bodies. Q (John de Lancie) from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is one of these beings, as is Trelane (William Campbell) from the original series. Those two beings tend to see corporeal humans as lesser species and amuse themselves by taunting and playing with them. Less whimsical is Kevin Uxbridge (John Anderson), a member of a powerful energy species called the Douwd. Kevin took the form of a human, married, and witnessed his wife killed, leading him to, in a moment of ill-temper, commit instant galaxy-wide genocide of a single species. He's the deadliest character in all of "Star Trek."

The list goes on. Q tormented the Calamarain, which exist as ionized gas. There are the Organians, the Lights of Zetar, and the godlike Metrons, the latter of whom oversaw the fight between Kirk (William Shatner) and the Gorn in the episode "Arena," and plenty of other examples. In most cases, non-corporeal entities are so far beyond human experience, it's difficult to communicate with them, much less come to some kind of diplomatic understanding.

But sometimes non-corporeal entities do become our friends. On "Star Trek: Prodigy," the character of Zero (Angus Imrie) is a Medusan who managed to construct a robot-like vehicle for themselves, allowing them to interact with us flesh-beings without exposing themselves. Sometimes the ineffability of the cosmos works in our favor.

Plenty of films left impressions on the 2026 movie schedule, but few managed to really hit the zeitgeist like Project Hail Mary did. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s science-fiction epic – based on Andy Weir’s 2021 book of the same name – managed to capture audiences’ imaginations (and make some solid money at the box office in the process). Anyone who needs further proof of the film’s popularity should know that a mixed-reality game is in the works and, to quote Rocky, the description of his role sounds “amaze.”

This new game – Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars – hails from game studio Maze Theory and takes place during a formerly untapped period of time within the main story. It specifically takes place after Dr. Ryland Grace saves his alien companion, Rocky, and before they return to the latter’s homeworld, Enid. Players take on the role of Dr. Ryland Grace (played by the impeccable and expressive Ryan Gosling in the film) and, as SFX Magazine on CinemaBlend learned from the developers, the game gets quite immersive.

Players can interact with objects, steer the titular ship (Hail Mary), repair it and even complete tasks like opening cupboards. One also only needs a headset to further immerse themselves in the game’s story, which was also talked out with Weir. Of course, all the while, fans can also interact with Rocky (who is not a pet) throughout their travels, and he’ll be actively watching your moves and providing feedback. Gameplay lead Sandy Lockie told SFX this about bringing Rocky and Grace’s relationship to the game:

We wanted to do justice to Rocky and Grace and their relationship. Sometimes they’ll be crabby with each other, sometimes they’ll get a little bit down and need the other one to pick them up.

It just wouldn’t have made sense to craft a game like this without including Rocky in some form or fashion. Since the film’s release he’s become something of a sensation, and he went viral after Amazon posted a video of the character watching himself. Even Neil DeGrasse Tyson praised the character’s design and noted that Weir and the filmmakers avoid the Hollywood trope of making him a humanoid. Judging by Lockie’s comments, even the Maze Theory team was taken with Rocky while they were testing the game:

Even when we’re testing, although you know he’s a character and isn’t really there, I’ll talk to him: ‘Well, what do I do here?’ He has good suggestions and sometimes bad suggestions. It’s one of those things that your brain just kind of lunges into, like, ‘Yep, Rocky’s there. He’s a character now!’ He’ll do jazz hands or prompt you to play rock-paper-scissors and all sorts of stuff . It’s fun to step into that and feel like he’s your friend and companion, your little explorer buddy.

All in all, this game should provide fans with a bit of a taste of being in Ryland’s shoes and present the opportunity to catch up with Rocky in some sense. Project Hail Mary’s ending may have closed the book on Grace and Rocky’s bromance for now, but I still like the idea of people being able to create their own moments reminiscent of the film’s best scenes. So, on that note, why not jump into this sweet-sounding extension of the PHM story?

Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars is now available Pico, Meta and Android XR. Also, fans can grab a Prime Video subscription and stream the movie on which the game is based right now.

#3531. Avril Lavigne Welcomes Her First Child At Age 42

Avril Lavigne is now a mom. The 42-year-old Canadian might count songs like "Here's to Never Growing Up" among her hits, but in news posted to Instagram Friday, Avril Lavigne revealed a very grown-up milestone.

Beneath a carousel of three black-and-white photos, Lavigne wrote “Our Mini Fucking Princess has arrived,” followed by emojis depicting a baby bottle, a crown, and a pink heart and bow. One photo shows Lavigne cradling an infant dressed in an animal-print onesie and matching headband, while another shows three pairs of Vans on a skateboard. No other details, including information on the baby's name or if Lavigne has a co-parent, were provided.

Avril Lavigne at the Viper Room in the early 2000s.

A spokesperson for the singer told People that “Avril has been enjoying time with her family while working on her new album and wants to thank the fans for all of their love!”

Lavigne has been married twice: once to Canadian guitarist Deryck Whibley and then to Chad Kroeger, the Canadian frontman of the band Nickelback. That latter partnership ended in 2018, but in 2022 she almost tied the knot a third time, with rapper Mod Sun. That relationship ended in 2023.

Mod Sun and Avril Lavigne attend the 2022 MTV Video Music Awards on August 28, 2022

One constant in Lavigne's life has been strong bond she shares with her parents. When, in May 2025, she brought her mother on stage at Madison Square Garden, she wrote on social media: “Ever since I was a little girl, both my mom and dad saw something in me and encouraged me to practice very hard and pursue my dream of becoming a singer/ musician. They made a lot of sacrifices for me and I could not be where I am today without them.”

Continuing, she wrote, “I am grateful to both my parents. Thank you for everything, I love you both!”

Lavigne was still a teenager when her parents allowed her to leave high school to pursue her dream, and her debut at age 17 was a smash hit. Her success continued with singles including 2002's chart-topper “Complicated" and 2021 song “Bite Me.”

Though Friday's announcement was a surprise to most, Lavigne has never been quiet about her desire to become a mom when the time is right. Speaking with E! News in 2013, she laid out her plan: "I want one or two [kids], but not right now," the then-29-year old said. "Like, in the future. Eventually."

#3530. Anne Hathaway's 2024 Romance Movie Is A Must-Watch For Colleen Hoover Fans

We're in a golden age of romance movies based on popular books, over which presides queen Colleen Hoover. There have been four movies based on Colleen Hoover novels and they've thus far ranged from sort of okay to entirely forgettable. But there's no denying it can be fun to settle down with a film you know is going to be absolute nonsense and just turn off your brain while two hot people fall in love and do it and stuff. Unfortunately, once you've watched the four Hoover films, you're stuck with the books until the author decides which of her stories to adapt next. In the meantime, may I direct your attention to a romance starring Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine, which at least tries to be more than an excuse for more hot people doing it scenes.

"The Idea of You" sees Hathaway falling for He-Man in a romantic comedy that, wouldn't you know it, is based on a book — because Hollywood will seemingly only green-light love stories if they've been pre-approved by BookTok. This one adapts actress turned author Robinne Lee's 2017 novel of the same name, in which she tackled the notion of women losing their desirability post-40. The movie similarly explores this idea via Hathaway and Galitzine's age gap relationship, and did so successfully for the most part.

Hathaway, of course, starred in the latest Hoover adaptation, the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which was helmed by "The Idea of You" director Michael Showalter. Sadly, for those expecting a fairly straightforward romance, the "Devil Wears Prada" star spent a good chunk of the movie sitting motionless and glaring at Dakota Johnson while she stole her husband. "The Idea of You," however, was a much better Showalter x Hathaway collab, and it's available to stream right now on Prime Video.

With its older-woman-falls-for-boy-band-singer narrative, you'd be forgiven for thinking "The Idea of You" is a movie that started as fanfiction. But in a 2024 TIME article, Robinne Lee pushed back against interpretations of her book being Harry Styles fanfiction and explained the real impetus for her story. "I was learning the hard way that in Hollywood, after 40, women are much less desirable," she wrote. "The assumption was that we ceased to be sexual beings and were thus less valuable. I was eager to prove the industry—and our culture at large—wrong, in my own little way." Lee, who criticized those who dubbed her book "fluff" or "fanfiction," saw her story as being about "a woman's midlife sexual awakening," and strove to ensure it was both "tantalizing and complex."

Much of that is preserved in the 2024 film adaptation, which Michael Showalter co-wrote with Jennifer Westfeldt. Anne Hathaway plays single mother and art gallery owner Solène Marchand, who accompanies her teenage daughter to Coachella. There, she meets Hayes Campbell (Nicholas Galitzine), the lead singer of boy band August Moon and all round handsome English gent. Despite there being several years between the two, Solène and Hayes share an instant connection and embark on a passionate love affair. But the latter's popstar status invites scrutiny, and as you might expect given Lee's explanation of her novel, most of it is an excuse to attack the 40-year-old Solène for being with a younger man and generally hurl misogynistic abuse.

Can the pair's relationship survive? You'll have to watch "The Idea of You" on Prime Video to find out — which, if you're reeling from the absolute nonsense that was "Verity," is well worth doing.

"The Idea of You" premiered at the 2024 South by Southwest film festival before going straight to Amazon Prime Video in May of that year. While that direct-to-streaming trajectory might typically indicate a less than stellar romantic comedy, "The Idea of You" actually earned some impressive reviews — a testament to Robinne Lee's efforts to go beyond your typical romantic fiction fare as well as Michael Showalter and Jennifer Westfeldt's ability to preserve that effort in their adaptation.

On Rotten Tomatoes, the film holds a very respectable 81% "certified fresh" critic score — a damn sight better than the 32% "Verity" managed to eke out. /Film's Ryan Scott was certainly impressed, writing in his "The Idea of You" review, "this is the genre at its best." Otherwise, reviewers were won over by Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine's chemistry and performances. That's to be expected in Hathaway's case. The actor is usually the best thing about any movie she's in, and while there are arguably more compelling modern Hathaway performances — her chilling 2023 thriller that flew completely under the radar, "Eileen," being one example — she does a fine job in "The Idea of You," conveying all the vulnerability and strength of the Solène Marchand in Lee's original novel.

Galitzine, meanwhile, is also perfectly charming if a bit too impressed with himself. The man is no stranger to romance stories, either, having starred alongside Netflix's romance queen Sofia Carson in 2022's "Purple Hearts" (watch that if you want a more straightforward romantic drama). Otherwise, "The Idea of You" is a great palette cleanser for recovering "Verity" viewers but should also go down well with Colleen Hoover fans craving a bit more romance from their Hathaway-led entertainment.

While it’s been over three decades since the final Full House episode aired, DJ Tanner actress Candace Cameron Bure still feels her TV “family” is important to her. So, you can only imagine how emotional the TV actress’s tribute was for her TV dad, Bob Saget, on the fourth anniversary of his death this year. If you want to get more in your feels, Bure shared her sweet reaction to BTS footage showing her and Saget on set. Fans, prepare to bring out the tissues.

Since Bob Saget died in 2022 due to accidental blunt head trauma, Candace Cameron Bure said it’s been hard watching Full House clips. But after ET showed her throwback clips from 1994 of her and Saget together on the set of the sitcom (as well as an earlier joint interview with John Stamos), it brought out all kinds of emotional, nostalgic feels:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

I just want to cry seeing the late stand-up comic introduce the former child star as his “TV daughter” as their arms are wrapped around each other. The emotions were already present when the Great American Media actress honored Saget through a series of photos. With each picture, it was clear that Saget didn't need to be Danny Tanner to show affection to his co-stars.

But seeing old clips of Saget with Bure reminded me why they made a great TV father/daughter duo on their show. Their familial chemistry on the ABC series was evident through every heartfelt talk, laugh and of course, hug.

As the former Hallmark Channel star was watching these clips, an emotional Bure revealed it was the first time she had ever seen them. While being “teary-eyed,” the Some Kind of Wonderful alum shared more about what she was thinking while reflecting on the good old days:

That was great! That was so fun to see. [...] Yeah, that was really emotional to see Bob. I just have so much love for him. I really do. He was such a good friend, such a loving person, and loved everyone so well. I miss him. I miss those hugs and the jokes.

The Full House alums truly appeared to have a friendship that stood the test of time. In fact, you could have called their friendship unlikely, as Bure couldn’t get into Saget's raunchy stand-up material. However, she said it was easy to be her TV dad’s friend, as she told herself to separate the comedian’s material from the "kindness" and "love" he brought out. Because the talented actress had known Saget since she was 11, it was no wonder they were still so close by the time the latter passed.

I’m glad that Candace Cameron Bure got to see her younger self with Bob Saget. As heartbreaking as it may be for me to watch those throwback clips, I’d like to believe it strengthens the love and memories she has with her old friend that’ll never go away. You can watch DJ and Danny navigate life together on Full House, which is streaming now with Disney+ subscription or an active Hulu subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3528. Los Javis Are “Living a Dream” As La Bola Negra with Penélope Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente, and Miguel Bernardeau Collects Honors

While La Bola Negra continues to amass various accolades and early awards, like the Best Director award at this year's Cannes Film Festival and the Audience Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo are extra grateful and overwhelmed by the film's reception and success in their home country of Spain.

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

“You can't plan the miracle,” Calvo said during a panel conversation moderated by Ricky Martin at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “We’ve done many projects and each one of them has, they've all been good, but you never know when it's going to happen. And with La Bola Negra, we thought it was a very specific story and we thought that our audience was going to like it, but we never knew it was going to hit everyone. I think it's about to become the second highest grossing movie in the history of Spain. For me, the most beautiful part of it is the videos of the people hugging after the screenings, giving tissues to each other, comforting each other.”

La Bola Negra follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War. The acclaimed Spanish language drama spans nearly a century and stars Miguel Bernardeau, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo (the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente) in his first major acting role, Carlos Gonzalez, Milo Quifes and Penélope Cruz.

Guitarricadelafuente at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Following an exclusive screening of the film on Friday, Martin moderated a panel conversation featuring directors Ambrossi and Calvo, and stars Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau. Calvo said they are all riding high on the positive audience reactions and reception. “Creating this sense of community and hearing people saying, ‘This movie changed me. It really made me understand things about me.’ The power that art has, we forget it, but then this happens and … the rest is a dream. The rest we're living is a dream.”

The directors also consider having Cruz play a small but pivotal role in the film to be part of their living a dream. When Martin asked Cruz how her longstanding allyship to the LGBTQ+ community shaped her intention or performance, she said, “I don't even ask myself that question because it's such a part of me, of the way that I was raised. My very young parents, my parents had me when they were 21. It was a house where the values were about respect and it was just like breathing. They didn't even have to sit us down and give us a lecture about it, it was the way my family was living by example. And on top of that, then I had my other master Pedro Almodóvar who I've worked with for seven movies. And I always remember growing up thinking, why is he not the president of our country? Because he was huge in a time where his presence was really necessary, not only through his films, but also by the things that he was saying. So I feel like all of that has shaped me.”

Miguel Bernardeau, Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz, Javier Calvo, Javier Ambrossi and Ricky Martin at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

She continued: “So when I have in my hands the possibility of playing somebody like Nené Romero, that is a reminder that unfortunately not everyone in the world feels the way we feel about everyone having a right for respect, everyone having a right to be themselves.”

Ricky Martin at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Martin, a Bola Negra superfan who admitted he was nervous to be asking questions instead of answering them, the actor and musician said he found out about his hosting opportunity only the day before and despite the nerves couldn't pass up the opportunity to help celebrate the film.

“I usually answer the questions, I never ask the questions, but I needed to be here,” he told the audience. “I saw this film and for a while I was in the movie. I was really touched. The acting, the way it was written, people are crying because that's just the way it is, [really moving].”

Miguel Bernardeau at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3527. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3526. Leonard Nimoy Loved This Star Trek Episode That Allowed Him To Show Off A Different Side Of Spock

What was Leonard Nimoy's favorite "Star Trek" episode? It's almost a trick question. Human beings are constantly changing and fickle creatures; the answer to our favorite anything can change depending on our moods. Nimoy, who played Spock for almost 50 years, couldn't be expected to give one consistent answer for that long.

But there are a few episodes that Nimoy consistently named among his favorites, including in his 1975 autobiography "I Am Not Spock." One of them was "This Side of Paradise," co-written by D. C. Fontana and Nathan Butler and one of the best Spock episodes of "Star Trek." The Enterprise visits colony world Omicron Ceti III, home to a plant species that secretes spores that take root in humanoid hosts. Once they do, the hosts remain in a state of perfect bliss, but they also lose all their ambition. (The story is a likely reference to the Lotus-Eaters in "The Odyssey.")

Spock is one of the infected. His stone face cracks into rubble as he becomes joyful, happily expressive, and even rekindles a romance with local botanist Leila Kalomi (Jill Ireland). Nimoy wrote in "I Am Not Spock" that he enjoyed the episode for showing Spock in a mood we almost never saw him — not coldly logical, sarcastic, or struggling to control his emotions, but genuinely carefree.

"This is a very special episode for me for obvious reasons and particularly because, where Spock was so totally adult in most of his attitudes and reactions throughout the series, this episode provided a chance to expose the complete child within. We saw him loving, picnicking, romping, and literally swinging playfully in the trees. It was a total exposure of internal Spock that so many people have always suspected was there."

Watching "This Side of Paradise" now, it might remind you of the Apple TV series "Pluribus," where all of humanity is turned into a blissful hive mind (collectively "The Others"). In "This Side of Paradise," strong negative emotions literally destroy the spores, which is also a weakness of the Others in "Pluribus."

In "This Side of Paradise," though, there's no identity theft. The spores let Spock be his innermost self. Compare other times we see Spock's emotions come out, like in "The Naked Time" where he cries over having never told his mother he loved her, or "Journey to Babel" where said mother, Amanda (Jane Wyatt), recounts how Spock used to cry because other Vulcan children bullied him. As only a half-Vulcan, Spock is especially self-conscious about living up to his people's teachings about logic.

When the spores hit him, those anxieties melt away. Note how Leila says to him he has "no need to hide [his] inner face anymore" and Spock says "I can love you," as if finally allowing himself something he'd previously denied.

Nimoy described other "Star Trek" episodes as favorites such as "Devil in the Dark," where the Enterprise crew visit a mining colony to find a creature killing the inhabitants. The culprit, a Horta (resembling a pile of living molten lava), is sentient and Spock telepathically communicates with it, discovering it was only acting to protect its offspring. Nimoy praised that one as a "wonderful episode about the fear of the unknown," and "Devil in the Dark" is known to be a favorite of William Shatner's, too.

"Devil in the Dark" and "This Side of Paradise" are very different episodes, but both ones anchored by Spock. Little surprise that Leonard Nimoy loved them.

Spoilers for Season 2, Episode 6 of Marshals are ahead! You can stream the series with a Paramount+ subscription and catch new episodes on CBS every Sunday.

The episode of Marshals that just aired on the 2026 TV schedule is inspired by a tragedy that actually happened to one of its stars and American Indian Affairs Coordinator, Mo Brings Plenty, and his family. In 2024, his nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, died, and a coroner ruled out foul play. His family disagreed with that, and they’re still looking for answers. In this week's episode of Marshals, Mo’s nephew, Troy, is found dead, and he and Kayce work to prove that it was a murder, not suicide. Ultimately, the case is left unsolved, and according to Mo Brings Plenty, that was a very important detail to include.

Knowing that “Roughstock” was inspired by his own experiences, I asked Mo Brings Plenty, who plays Mo in Marshals and Yellowstone, about details in the episode he was happy to see included. He immediately noted that he was glad the case was left unsolved, because that kind of outcome happens in real life, often, as the actor explained:

Oh, I was happy to see that when the police officer said he just kind of blew it off, because that's really the case. And so I was happy that we showed that legitimate part of it. Not every officer is that way, but in some cases, in some states - primarily states that have a high American Indian population - that occurs.

When I spoke to Mo in March this year about an episode of Marshals having to do with missing American Indians, he told me they “haven’t got any answers for” what happened to his nephew, Cole.

In this episode of Marshals, it’s made very clear that while Troy’s case will stay open, it will likely go unsolved. It’s obvious that it’s not being prioritized by law enforcement, and despite the marshals best efforts, there is no solution as to who killed Troy by the end of the episode. When I asked Mo why it was important for this episode to go without a solution to Troy’s case, he said:

Because the wheel of justice doesn't turn for us as American Indian people, and of course we're tax-paying people as well. And so, you know, first responders get their funding through taxpayers, tax funding, and so when it doesn't work for us, then it's so frustrating. It's like, ‘Well, why are we even paying taxes?’ And so that's one of the things that is impactful for me, and that I need to continue to speak about because it is occurring.

In the case of Mo’s real nephew, Cole, he was found dead a few days after he was reported missing and named as a suspect in a domestic violence case. Two years later, Mo spoke to THR and claimed that his nephew’s death had gone “uninvestigated,” while the Lawrence Police Department said there was “no foul play involved in Cole’s death.”

When I spoke to Mo about this topic recently and how it was represented on this Yellowstone show, he said:

It's sad for me and my family, especially when I hear the cry for other nationalities and in foreign countries, when the very same thing is occurring to us as the original inhabitants within this country, we're basically flying over mission fields to get to mission fields.

According to the U.S. Department of the Interior Indian Affairs, there are “approximately 4,200 missing and murder cases that have gone unsolved.” And when I asked Mo Brings Plenty if Marshals could ever circle back to Troy’s unsolved case, he said:

Absolutely, it could definitely happen. But you know, there are so many stories. I mean, my family is not the only family. This isn't the first time something like this has occurred in real life. You know, there are many stories, many families, different situations, different circumstances that are going through the same thing.

Overall, he was clear that there are lots of stories like his that should be shown on Kayce’s Yellowstone spinoff. He’s not the only one who has lost a loved one in this way and was left without answers, and he’s hoping to see more of those stories depicted on Marshals.

Now, to see how Mo’s story continues, you can watch the next episode of Marshals on November 22 at 8:30 p.m. ET, and you can stream it the next day on Paramount+.

#3524. Zara Tindall Shows Cheltenham Why She's The Queen of Race Day Dressing

Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II brought a dash of regal glamour to the proceedings following a glitzy night out in support of Prince William.

And while the sun may have been out, the Olympic equestrian still needed to wrap up against the chill. Tindall opted for a long plaid coat from L'Agence, a Purdey roll-neck jumper in brown, and a fascinator from Sally-Ann Provan. She accessorized with a new pair of Hector Lion earrings, a new Fairfax & Favor handbag, and completed the look with leather boots, also from Fairfax & Favor.

Zara Tindall joined in the action at Cheltenham Racecourse on Friday

Dolly, on the other hand, wore an avant-garde feather coat with knee-high boots and what looked to be a pair of emerald tights.

The pair were last spotted together in October, when they attended the William Hill Showcase Meeting at Cheltenham, but their friendship goes way back. Long considered Zara’s best friend, Dolly became Princess Anne’s lady-in-waiting in 2024. A former NHS midwife, she helped to deliver Zara’s third child, Lucas Tindall, on the floor of Zara’s bathroom at Gatcombe Park after the plan for the birth went awry in 2021.

Jade Holland Cooper and Zara Tindall on day one of The November Meeting at Cheltenham racecourse

But Dolly’s bond with the niece of King Charles III goes back long before that. (Not for nothing did Zara’s husband, Mike Tindall, joke that the 53-year-old is “more important than I am.”) Dolly was Zara’s maid of honor when the pair tied the knot, and when Zara split from her then-fiancé, jockey Richard Johnson, in 2003, the pair moved in together—they still live close by in the Cotswolds.

Having worked as a maternity practitioner in the NHS in Gloucestershire for 13 years, Dolly also did some philanthropic work using her maternity expertise, working in the unit of a hospital in Kambia, Sierra Leone for a month in 2013. At Kambia, she taught staff basic nursing skills. Before qualifying as a nurse, Dolly studied fashion and Cordon Bleu cookery at Eastbourne College of Food and Fashion, graduating in 1989.

Zara Tindall also braved the stormy weather for a day at Cheltenham with Dolly in October

Dolly Maude is known for her love of horses—a passion she shares with Zara and Princess Anne—and is often seen in Ascot’s royal box alongside the Princess Royal. In March 2024, she made her first official appearance as the Princess Royal’s lady-in-waiting, a momentous occasion that marked a new phase of her enduring bond with the royal family.

The royal confidant has four children with her husband Chris: Billy, who studied at Swansea University; Nell, who trained at the Central School of Ballet; a keen skier, Ted; and Mary.

Princess Anne's daughter wrapped up in a warm plaid coat and roll-neck jumper

Concerning Dolly’s appointment, another friend of Mrs. Maude's told The Telegraph, “She’s such a great girl. For the Princess Royal, it’s a perfect fit because of their shared love of dogs and horses. She’s not only extremely close to Zara, she also gets on brilliantly with the Princess. She’s fiercely loyal and discreet. It’s a great match.”

While much of Zara Tindall’s time this season has been spent touring the country’s most prestigious racing meets, she still found time to support her cousin, Prince William, at one of his treasured annual traditions. The Prince of Wales helped to put together the Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles on Wednesday night and invited Zara to the celebration of conservation, alongside Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer and the Marchioness of Bath.

Dolly Maud made her debut as lady-in-waiting for the Princess Royal at the 2024 Commonwealth Day Service in March

Zara showcased her characteristically elegant style, donning a sapphire-blue Rebecca Vallance short-sleeved midi number, aptly named the “Crown Jewel” dress, which she paired with Kiki McDonough earrings. It is not the first time that the royal has lent her support to Prince William’s second-longest patronage: she also joined the crowd at the Tusk Awards in 2025, donning Rebecca Vallance again, and tearing up at the Prince of Wales’ speech in honor of those who gave their lives as rangers.
