#3523. 7 Upcoming Sci-Fi Series, Ranked By Hype (2026 and Early 2027)

Sci-fi lovers are going to be spoilt for choice

Why do sci-fi shows generate such massive hype? A select few, like Fallout or Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, bank on pre-existing fanbases, but most genre titles are highly anticipated purely due to their exciting premise. Stories about technological collapse or corporate overreach feel urgent and relevant, while dystopian cautionary tales are a fun way to explore speculative scenarios. Sci-fi also promises intricate world-building, be it through grounded space settings like The Expanse or alternative timeline tales like For All Mankind.

Sci-fi is also as versatile as it gets. Shows like Paradise blend action-thriller elements with a puzzle-box narrative that sparks enthusiastic theorycrafting and discussion. There’s also hype surrounding talented showrunners like Vince Gilligan (Pluribus) or Jonathan Nolan (Westworld), who never fail to push the limits of the genre in intriguing ways. With that in mind, here are seven upcoming sci-fi shows that are highly anticipated for a plethora of reasons, ranked by hype.

Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner paved the way for commercially viable cyberpunk media, becoming one of the most influential sci-fi movies of all time. Its sequel, Blade Runner 2049, etched a flawed legacy with an interesting continuation of its complex themes. Prime Video’s upcoming series, Blade Runner 2099, presents a unique scenario: What would the world look like when the replicants take over?

This premise completely flips the status quo of previous entries. Humans are now second-class citizens and replicant blade runners are at the top of society. Apart from boasting a star-studded cast, Blade Runner 2099 has secured Scott’s involvement as executive producer, with production designer Paul Inglis (Game of Thrones) creating the tactile world of the show. These are great reasons to look forward to a show that seems to be subverting franchise expectations by daring to do something unexpected.

Another Ridley Scott film offshoot, Noah Hawley’s Alien: Earth was a pleasant surprise for several reasons. The show was the first to streamline sprawling franchise lore into the television format, and did so by radically evolving the existing storyline. Season 1 opens in the year 2120, two years before Scott’s Alien, when a research vessel with extraterrestrial specimens — including a Xenomorph — crash-lands into a major metropolitan area.

Hawley introduces a completely fresh setting that allows new characters to assume the stage. There’s also more room to explore unethical corporate motivations, like the consciousness of terminally ill children being used as fighter units inside synthetic bodies. Alien: Earth also questions who the real “monster” is. Although a gnarly creature feature that isn’t afraid to indulge in all-out action and body horror, the show ultimately lingers on the inhumane nature of hyper-capitalism and corporate greed. Season 1 ends on an exciting cliffhanger, making the anticipation for the next season feel earned and well-founded.

No matter how flawed a Star Wars show may be, it ends up generating enough hype for both long-time fans and casual viewers to tune in. The case for Ahsoka is unique, as its hype rests on existing animated entries like The Clone Wars and Star Wars: Rebels, with Ahsoka Tano (Rosario Dawson) being a beloved character. Season 1 of Ahsoka feels like a live-action Rebels at certain points, especially with the presence of legacy characters like Anakin Skywalker (Hayden Christensen) and Ezra Bridger (Eman Esfandi).

Season 2’s major draw is Grand Admiral Thrawn (Lars Mikkelsen), an iconic villain who poses a grave threat as a remnant of the Galactic Empire. This is pretty high-stakes from a lore perspective, as the show has the opportunity to expand franchise mythology like never before. Ahsoka’s identity as a Jedi also carries great nuance, just like the complexity granted to her ex-padawan, Sabine Wren (Natasha Liu Bordizzo). Excitement over major space battles and lightsaber duels is a given, along with meaningful character growth that will potentially enhance what we already know.

Liu Cixin’s Remembrance of Earth’s Past book trilogy has been adapted into 3 Body Problem, which is set to return with a high-budget second season and enhanced stakes. Game of Thrones showrunners David Benioff and D. B. Weiss managed to streamline the sprawling novels into a memorable first season so far, although opinions remain divided on pacing and characterization. Even so, 3 Body Problem accomplishes the challenging task of conveying the high-concept ideas that drive the books, creating a compelling puzzle-box narrative that has kept audiences hooked.

Season 1 establishes astrophysicist Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao) and her motivations to invite an alien race known as the San-Ti to invade Earth. A group of friends known as the Oxford Five get involved in the mystery, unraveling more about the San-Ti through a mysterious virtual reality game. Season 2 is set to revolve around the Dark Forest hypothesis, potentially leaning into hard sci-fi concepts such as the three-body problem and quantum entanglement. As Cixin’s trilogy is sweeping in scope and tone, it is natural to expect the same from 3 Body Problem.

Dystopian sci-fi shows are dime a dozen, but Silo has managed to set itself apart over the course of three seasons. Its fourth and final season is the most anticipated, set to pay off an elaborate narrative setup at the end of the third season. Silo is about the titular underground silo with 144 levels, whose current inhabitants believe that the structure has been built to protect them from the toxic environment outside. After the death of the silo’s sheriff, engineer Juliette Nichols (Rebecca Ferguson) embarks on a long and arduous journey to uncover the truth.

Silo has always been a slow-burn affair. The fourth season is expected to answer burning questions that have been posed since the first season, such as the true purpose of the silo project. As the show is based on Hugh Howey’s book trilogy, there’s hope for a meaningful, structured ending that reflects the consistent quality of the show. It is also fair to assume that Silo will close out on an emotional note, as the extreme nature of the conflict is bound to rack up casualties or put our favorite characters in danger.

Isaac Asimov’s Foundation has been adapted into an excellent Apple TV show by David S. Goyer and Josh Friedman. A tyrannical Empire rules most of the known galaxy, thanks to a triumvirate of leaders who are clones of a long-deceased Emperor. The premise hinges on Professor Hari Seldon (Jared Harris), who devises a mathematical technique called psychohistory that allows him to predict the future. After discovering the Empire’s inevitable downfall and the eventual birth of a new era, he sets out to shorten the upcoming dark ages.

Season 4 will veer into fresh directions, as new showrunners Ian Goldberg and David Kob will take over while still sticking to the core blueprint for the evolving story. The previous season also ended with a massive bait-and-switch, completely subverting expectations and our understanding of how psychohistory works. The fourth season will also draw from Asimov’s Second Foundation, which widens the story and heralds the return of certain fan-favorite characters.

William Gibson’s Neuromancer is a cornerstone cyberpunk novel, and its long-awaited Apple TV adaptation looks promising so far. Gibson’s prose is notoriously difficult to translate to the screen, which makes Neuromancer all the more exciting for attempting to do the impossible. The story opens with super hacker Case (Callum Turner), a down-on-his-luck man with a damaged spinal cord that blocks him from accessing this world's version of the internet, known as "the Matrix." Desperate to survive, Case agrees to carry out a risky heist for a shady individual known as Armitage (Mark Strong), who is hiding a world of secrets in a story built on deception.

Cyberpunk owes a lot to Neuromancer, as everything from "cyberspace" to the act of “jacking in” to the net was introduced in Gibson’s novel. These concepts are not novel anymore, but the show has the unique opportunity to showcase why this particular story is worth telling. This is a story about tech anxieties, corporate surveillance, and rogue artificial intelligence — themes that are more relevant today than ever before. That unprecedented timeliness, combined with the show’s potential to introduce something unprecedented to the cyberpunk genre, makes Neuromancer the most hyped sci-fi show in the near future.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3522. This Christian Bale Western Drama Flopped In Theaters But Is Worth Revisiting

For a long time it seemed as though audiences might see Clint Eastwood and John Wayne team up in what could have been the greatest Western ever made. That long-gestating, never-realized project was set to be called "Hostiles" and was supposed to be based on a script by Larry Cohen. Alas, the Duke remained entirely against collaborating with a spiritual successor so opposed to his traditionalist roots, and the film was never made. In 2017, however, we did get a movie called "Hostiles" which had similarly languished as a semi-finished script for years. This film had nothing to do with the planned Eastwood/Wayne vehicle, but it did focus on two seemingly opposed parties who find common ground as their harrowing story plays out on the plains of the Old West.

"Hostiles" stars Christian Bale as a United States Army cavalry officer forced to escort a Cheyenne war chief across the dangerous terrain of 1892 America. It's written and directed by Scott Cooper who most recently oversaw Jeremy Allen White's haunted performance in "Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere." Prior to that, Cooper worked with Bale on the 2013 crime drama "Out of the Furnace" and in 2015 he directed "Black Mass," the Johnny Depp-led crime drama based on real life mobster Whitey Bulger.

"Hostiles" came directly after "Black Mass" in Cooper's filmography, and saw him re-team with Bale for a film that was well received by critics despite being a box office disappointment. Today, the film barely gets a mention. But it should, as Cooper and Bale managed to deliver a taut Western drama that was worthy of far more attention than it got from mass audiences.

In 2017, Christian Bale led the weary and grim "Hostiles," a film that very nearly made our best dark Westerns list. Set in 1892, it follows Bale's Army Captain Joseph Blocker, who's nearing retirement and looking forward to leaving his military years behind him. But President Benjamin Harrison has one more job for Blocker. Before he's allowed to retire, he must escort a cancer-stricken Cheyenne war chief named Yellow Hawk (Wes Studi) and his family from Fort Berringer, New Mexico to his tribal lands in Montana. Bale's Army Captain initially refuses on the grounds that he and Yellow Hawk are old enemies. But he's coerced into accepting the job and sets out on the perilous journey.

Along the way he meets widow Rosalee Quaid (Rosamund Pike), who joins the group on a trek that becomes increasingly dangerous. As such, despite their differences, Blocker, Yellow Hawk, and their cohorts must come together to survive a harsh and unforgiving landscape.

As Deadline noted in 2018, "Hostiles" is based on an old manuscript from Donald E. Stewart. The screenwriter, who passed away in 1999, penned the Oscar-Winning 1982 biographical thriller "Missing" and the 1990s Jack Ryan films: "The Hunt for Red October," "Patriot Games," and "Clear and Present Danger." During the '80s, Stewart also wrote a version of what became "Hostiles," which came to Cooper by way of Stewart's widow. It seems she came across the manuscript while packing to move house, and having been impressed by "Out of the Furnace," sent it to Scott Cooper in the hope he could finally realize her late husband's vision.

Upon reading Donald E. Stewart's "Hostiles" manuscript, Scott Cooper decided to expand upon what he called the "kernel of an idea about a man who, in Christian Bale's character, has been indoctrinated by the United States government from a very young age essentially to fight and to kill." Thus began the process of finally bringing "Hostiles" to the big screen. Sadly, when it finally did hit theaters, the movie grossed just $35.7 million on what Deadline claims was a $39 million budget (The Hollywood Reporter put the budget at $50 million).

On the plus side, "Hostiles" did earn a respectable 71% Rotten Tomatoes score. It isn't the finest score, but not only did the film make /Film's best Westerns of the 21st Century list, RT isn't the most nuanced indicator of how critics actually feel about the movies they review. In other words, whether "Hostiles" is, in fact, one of the best Westerns of this century depends on who you ask. Richard Whittaker of the Austin Chronicle, for instance, found "Hostiles" to be "timeless yet contemporary," and praised the film for "diving headlong into the ongoing and often horrific impact of the United States' policies and attitudes to indigenous culture." Dan Jolin of Empire, meanwhile, called Christian Bale's performance "astounding." On the other hand, the San Francisco Chronicle's Mick LaSalle was unimpressed with the film's "dull characters," an "almost-endless tedium" and its "nihilistic violence."

The only way to know for sure where you stand on this mostly overlooked Bale-led Western is to check it out for yourself. Unfortunately, the film isn't streaming anywhere at the time of writing, but can be rented for a reasonable price from the usual digital platforms.

#3521. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3519. As Hollywood Battles AI, Pedro Pascal Says Making Behemoth! Filled Him with “a Tremendous Amount of Hope”

Pedro Pascal says that the character he plays in Behemoth!, his first leading film role, is the “closest thing to me that I’ve ever done.” And because of this, “the experience on set felt surreal in a sort of physically tangible way,” Pascal told the audience during a Q&A at Vanity Fair’s Screening Room at LACMA on Saturday.

Directed by Tony Gilroy, Behemoth! tells the story of Alex, a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and the world of Hollywood film scoring after decades performing symphonic work around the country.

“The mixing of my own life and this person's life, I've lived a very nomadic one. Don't ask me where home is. And so that felt like it was crossing personal lines for me in a way,” he continued during a post-screening discussion about the film, which featured Pascal and writer-director Tony Gilroy, moderated by VF's West Coast Editor John Ross.

Tony Gilroy and Pedro Pascal  at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

But according to Gilroy, their collaboration on the film almost didn't happen, thanks to an alleged missed connection at a Star Wars event.

“We went to a Star Wars convention in Tokyo where we took Andor,” recalled Gilroy. “There was this big Disney dinner so all the Star Wars people are there and [Pascal] was kind of busy and flighty.”

“I had the flu! I flew from London to Tokyo!” Pascal countered.

Gilroy continued: “He seemed like he was so hip that he didn't come to the dinner. I thought, 'Oh he's got such a great thing going on he's going to some better party; he's not going to a boring dinner.'”

As the audience laughed, Pascal was quick to set the record straight: “I cannot believe that you thought that I ditched that dinner. I was doing re-shoots of Fantastic Four!” he said. “They flew me to Tokyo that night and flew me back and I was on a set. [Turns toward the audience] Can you believe this?”

“Oh my God. I'm calling Kathy Kennedy [the President of Lucasfilm] right away,” Gilroy joked.

Luckily, the moviemaking stars (and schedules) aligned and the pair was able to make their personal, moving film with Pascal serving as Gilroy's “exclamation point. He has all the sadness and all the covering that this character needs to have and the nomadic life.”

Pedro Pascal, Tony Gilroy and John Ross at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Pascal and Gilroy formed a genuine bond and are very comfortable making playful jabs at each other, keeping things light but also expressing their gratitude for being able to make Behemoth! their way, in Los Angeles, where the film and television industry has been struggling to regain a foothold. Despite the challenges, past and present, they are holding out hope for human-made storytelling to foster further human connection.

“People's natural resistance to the robot takeover is clear,” said Gilroy when asked about the rise of AI. “I don't know what's going to happen. I really don't. The music scene out here is the coral reef of what's happened. It's been dying out here for the last 15 years… It's grooving a little bit now. I think people want humans. I don't know what's going to come back, but this is this incredibly humanizing element of movies that's happened. Can it be replaced by AI? Probably, quite shockingly, simply. There's probably an emotional amplitude knob on some f—ing algorithm, but this movie is organic.”

Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy  at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Pascal walked away from Behemoth! feeling optimistic. “The experience of shooting this movie definitely injected me with a tremendous amount of hope,” he said. “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious. And it was primarily locations, and so Los Angeles was just constantly revealing itself in all of these magical ways because we were so location-based. I had shot a series in Colombia for three seasons, and I would argue that the primary character of that series, Narcos, was shooting it in the country of Colombia because there was only one way of capturing that energy and that physical story. And LA did that as well. And then it's so tender. I think the story is incredibly tender. Would you ever expect it from this guy [gestures to Gilroy]?”

“Oh my God. What a cold, weird thing to say,” the director joked.

“There are other movies this year that I think in their own way, movies that I've seen this year that I love so much, that fight for humanity and the storytelling,” Pascal continued. “So I think that there is a sort of pushback that could be really, really thrilling as far as [creativity] is concerned, as far as politics is concerned. We want to be human beings and we want to be connected to one another and we want to tell each other's stories and witness each other's stories and we want to look after each other and all that shit. That's my hope.”

Tony Gilroy at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Gilroy had another suggestion: “Blow up the AI centers, man," he joked. “I don't mean to blow them up. I mean blow them up at the voting box. Go and vote and blow them up. Go see the Musk documentary, man. Go see that, watch the whole four hours. I'm pitching my movie [here], but watch that movie.”

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3518. 10 Best Western Movie Gunfights Of All Time, Ranked

While Westerns boast breathtakingly rustic vistas and memorably rugged main characters, chances are, we're there to see some sharpshooting gunplay. Many Western movies that everyone should watch at least once are anchored by a riveting action set piece between frontier gunfighters. These sequences range from drawn-out battles throughout harsh landscapes and dusty towns to quick-draw showdowns over in a single burst of gunfire. We're looking back at personal favorite gunfights in the history of Western movies, each earning a spot in cinematic history.

Silver screen legends like John Wayne and Clint Eastwood immortalized themselves through the gunfight scenes in Westerns they starred in. In many cases, the single most iconic scene in a given Western is its gunslinging action sequence. After all, the Wild West archetype is one revolving around its laconic gunfighters, not its bucolic communities on the fringes of civilization.

With those qualities in mind, these are the best Western movie gunfights of all time ranked, epitomizing the genre's gunslinging appeal.

So much of the classic 1953 Western "Shane" is the build-up to its titular protagonist finally showing everyone what he's got. Played by Alan Ladd, the character is a drifter with a mysterious past who comes to work on a farm on the frontier. When these homesteads are targeted by an unscrupulous land baron, Shane's lethal skills quickly come in handy. This comes to a quick-draw climax as Shane kills the murderous crook along with his sadistic hired gun Jack Wilson (Jack Palance), though Shane himself is wounded.

Ladd's Shane is the ultimate gunslinger archetype, though he really only gets one gunfight in the entire movie. Fortunately, "Shane" makes this sequence count, with this violent inevitability expertly staged and crafted. To heighten the mood, much of this climax is filmed in a shadowy saloon as Shane overcomes the obvious trap that he knowingly walks into. Fans still debate over 70 years later if Shane survived this gunfight, which is a testament to how memorable the sequence and its ambiguous aftermath are.

Even though it became a Western that flopped at the box office, the 2007 remake of "3:10 to Yuma" does its 1957 predecessor proud. That said, the difference between the two movies are most acutely felt in how they each end. The 2007 remake features farmer Dan Evans (Christian Bale) escorting outlaw Ben Wade (Russell Crowe) to a train station, with Ben begrudgingly going along for the last run. What follows is a running gunfight against those trying to stop Dan, who still finds the time to convince Ben to cooperate.

The last few minutes of the "3:10 to Yuma" remake are its most exciting, while filmmaker James Mangold still delivers on its main character arcs. Any sense of triumph is quickly undercut by the movie's tragic conclusion, differentiating it from both its short story source material and the 1957 film. The movie handles that fake-out marvelously while not mitigating the excitement that came before during this desperate run. Easily one of the greatest Western movies of the 2000s, "3:10 to Yuma" saves its best for last.

For as breezy as the overall movie is, the most well-known scenes in "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" are its most relentlessly intense. Though the duo being pursued by a posse across the Wild West for their train robberies stands out, the movie's ending is arguably its most famous sequence. Having relocated to Bolivia to resume their criminal activities, Butch (Paul Newman) and the Sundance Kid (Robert Redford) are ambushed by the authorities and take shelter in a nearby building. Charging outside, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid go out in a blaze of glory, with the movie ending on a freeze-frame as the pair are gunned down.

The alternate ending of "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" thankfully wasn't used, which would've actually shown its likable duo gruesomely killed. Instead, the scene leaves the carnage to the audience's imagination, rather than treading the same territory as the ending of "Bonnie & Clyde." That freeze-frame approach works well for the overall movie, giving the story its inevitable ending but without dwelling on the violence, staying in line with its general tone. The only gunfight on this list which doesn't show its decisive salvo on-screen, "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" focuses on its title characters' legend rather than its tragedy.

John Wayne led a lot of different Western movie gunfights, from classic quick-draws in "The War Wagon" to shadowy shootings in "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance." But the Wayne-starring gunfight that stands out from the rest of his work is his climactic confrontation in "True Grit." Wayne plays U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn in the 1969 movie, finally catching up with a crew of outlaws he had been pursuing for the entire film. After being insulted by the gang's leader Ned Pepper (Robert Duvall), an incensed Cogburn charges them alone with a gun in each hand and his horse's reins in his teeth.

John Wayne considered "True Grit" to be his first decent role in 20 years, and his one-man charge cements his character's place in his legacy. The action sequence isn't just the movie at its most rousing, and it shows a more ornery side to Wayne's usual frontier archetype. Expertly twirling his rifle in one hand to chamber a new round, just as he did in "Stagecoach" three decades prior, Wayne hasn't lost a step. Putting a furiously gun-toting Wayne back in the saddle, "True Grit" proved this old dog still had some new tricks.

Over a decade later, "Django Unchained" is still Quentin Tarantino's biggest movie, at least from a commercial standpoint. The final act of the 2012 movie takes place in Candyland, a notoriously brutal plantation run by the cruel slave owner Calvin Candie (Leonardo DiCaprio). Subjected by Calvin's nightmarish hospitality in an effort to rescue Brunhilda (Kerry Washington), the enslaved wife of Django (Jamie Foxx), King Schultz (Christoph Waltz) kills Calvin. This kickstarts a particularly blood-soaked gunfight, as Schultz is killed and Django battles gunmen around the plantation, until he is eventually forced to surrender.

The sanguine shootout may not be the final showdown in "Django Unchained," but it's a scene that we wish would never end. After the smug cruelty that Django and Schultz endure in Candyland, the action sequence feels like a cathartic release as Django exacts comeuppance on his hosts. To heighten the effusive enjoyment of the scene, Tarantino uses "Unchained (The Payback/Untouchable)" by James Brown and Tupac, while making every bullet hit like an artillery shell. The best gunfight that Tarantino has filmed to date, "Django Unchained" has its titular hero bring bloody retribution to its main villain's antebellum lair.

For much of "Unforgiven," the violent backstory of outlaw Will Munny (Clint Eastwood) was only hinted at, with Munny himself focused on being a farmer and single father. After learning that his old friend Ned Logan (Morgan Freeman) was murdered by the sadistic sheriff Little Bill Daggett (Gene Hackman), with his body mockingly displayed, Munny's lethal demeanor resurfaces. Storming into Little Bill's saloon, Munny shoots him and several of his associates, maintaining a clear-eyed, if furious, focus. After finishing off Little Bill, Munny threatens everyone to properly bury Logan or experience his wrath again before departing from the rainy frontier town for good.

The "Unforgiven" ending reveals that some legends are better left to fade away, and Munny is every inch the killer that he was reputed to be. Moreover, Munny inadvertently demonstrates Little Bill's own insight against him, staying calm and collected during the chaos of the gunfight, allowing him to take down all his enemies. Keeping in tone with the rest of the revisionist Western nature of the movie, this burst of violence isn't particularly flashy or stylized. But that makes the carnage all the more grounded and with understated menace as Eastwood delivers his definitive word on the genre that made him a star.

The most famous shootout in real Wild West history was the gunfight at the O.K. Corral in 1881 between the Cowboy outlaw gang and lawmen led by Wyatt Earp. Though this fateful showdown has been dramatized plenty of times in Western movies, the most entertaining depiction is in "Tombstone." Roughly serving as the centerpiece of the movie, the scene only lasts less than a minute, like the historical event. Several of the outlaws are killed in the exchange, while both of Wyatt's brothers are wounded before inciting the wrath of the other gang members.

"Tombstone" presents its historical figures in a stylized and colorful light, helping make it one of the best Western movies of the 1990s. Comparatively, the gunfight at the O.K. Corral is played relatively straight, which helps it stand out from the rest of the movie. The action is quick, brutal, and consequential, setting in motion the back half of the movie's stakes. Certainly one of the best gunfights in a relatively modern Western movie, "Tombstone" knows a lot is riding on its marquee confrontation and delivers accordingly.

The single most recognizable shot in Sergio Leone's "Once Upon a Time in the West" is the sight of three gunmen confronting Harmonica (Charles Bronson) at a train station. The scene opens the film, playing out largely with diegetic noise as the three gunfighters await the incoming train with their target. This sets the stage for Harmonica's arrival, earning his nickname from his first appearance with a screeching melody played from his mouth organ. Unfazed that he's outnumbered three-to-one, Harmonica takes his position against his three enemies and guns them all down singlehandedly though wounded in the skirmish.

"Once Upon a Time in the West" is bookended with genre-defining gunfights, but the opening sequence is the superior of the two. Leone's masterful positioning his actors in frame and suspense building until the inevitable draw finally punctuates that crescendo with a single exchange of gunfire. With Leone, it was all about finding ways to fuel that tension before letting it finally go off like a pressure cooker, a lesson that has visibly influenced Quentin Tarantino. "Once Upon a Time in the West" is among Charles Bronson's best movies and seeing him anchor the movie's opening gunfight sets the mood for Leone's requiem to the genre.

If "Once Upon a Time in the West" is best known for its opening, the following year's "The Wild Bunch" is best known for its ending. The movie follows a group of aging American outlaws in the early 20th century, led by Pike Bishop (William Holden), who flee to Mexico after a botched bank heist. The ensemble get caught up in the revolution south of the border, culminating in the quartet making their last stand against the full might of the Mexican army. Gathering around a machine gun emplacement, the group are eventually overwhelmed and killed but not before massacring scores of soldiers.

The gruesome to "The Wild Bunch" was reportedly as brutal to film as it was to watch, heightening the verisimilitude of the sequence. In a matter of seconds, this situation escalates out of control, full of fire and fury as Pike and his associates stand in the face of oblivion. There's no mistaking that these four men are marching quietly to their deaths, but as the scene reveals, they're going out on their own terms and they're not going alone. More than just the tale of four old outlaws, "The Wild Bunch" signals that the Wild West era didn't die out peacefully but with a violent fire in its guts.

Of course a Clint Eastwood Western was going to top this list, and of course it was going to be "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly." Virtually every Sergio Leone Western, like "Once Upon a Time in the West," has a standout shootout sequence, but the greatest is in his 1966 epic. The movie reaches its crescendo when it brings its titular trio together in a sprawling cemetery as they search for a hidden stash of loot. With the three gunslingers at odds, the characters have a tense staredown before Blondie (Eastwood) guns down Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef).

Powered by a stirring score by Ennio Morricone, the climax is one of the most effectively staged sequences Leone has ever directed. The intercutting of close-ups between the three main characters before being punctuated by a single burst of gunfire with mounting suspense all the while is masterfully done. The moment also provides Blondie with another opportunity to pull a fast one on Tuco (Eli Wallach), secretly unloading his pistol for the duel. The quick-draw gunfight that epitomizes Leone's meticulous style, "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" ends on a truly iconic note.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. #3516. Critical Role Returns With the Mighty Nein Season 2 in 2027, but Fans Aren’t Happy

More Mighty Nein is never a bad thing, but this latest news has left Critters despondent

It's always a great time to be a Critical Role fan, and 2027 will be no different, with several new live-play shows and series planned. However, things are about to get even better, thanks to a new announcement made by Critical Role during TwitchCon 2026: The Mighty Nein season 2 will arrive on Prime Video on March 24, 2027.

The news was announced during a special live Lord of the Rings one-shot, when Game Master Liam O’Brien asked fans to raise a cup to celebrate The Mighty Nein’s return.

However, the good news came with a worrying catch. According to the official news release, the episode release schedule for The Mighty Nein will be very different from that of its first season — and Critters are concerned about what this could mean for the show's future.

Season 2 of The Mighty Nein will consist of eight episodes, all of which will be released at once when the season debuts on Mar. 24, 2027. This contrasts sharply with the release schedule for season 1, which released its first three episodes on Nov. 19, 2025, followed by weekly episodes through Dec. 22, 2025.

The change has left Critters speculating whether Prime Video — the publisher and partner behind The Mighty Nein and Critical Role’s other animated series, The Legend of Vox Machina — has lost faith in Critical Role’s animated tales set in Exandria.

“God, I hope not,” one user posted on social media platform X, referring to all episodes of The Mighty Nein dropping at once. “Publishers have to know by now that dropping everything at once instantly kills a series online presence?”

“[It] makes me sad and I hope also isn't a choice that's at all indicative of Amazon's faith in the series or a sign s1 underperformed,” another user posted. “Really hope it means nothing at all and they just thought it'd do better bc tm9 is genuinely so good so far.”

It’s impossible to know what Prime Video is thinking about its binge release of The Mighty Nein, but Critters aren’t wrong. This type of release rarely sparks discussion the way a week-to-week release does.

Primve Video’s news release for season 2 of The Mighty Nein included a plot summary, which you can read below.

“In Season Two, The Mighty Nein set off on a pirate adventure across the high seas as they face their complicated pasts and hurtle toward a treacherous future. While Fjord’s burgeoning powers tempt him down a dark path, the Beacon reveals its own enticing possibilities, and the group must choose between newfound magic and their friendship.”

The first season of The Mighty Nein already featured plenty of changes, including a revised backstory for Aasimar barbarian Yasha (Ashley Johnson). There seem to be even more changes this time around, with the group’s pirate arc taking center stage earlier than expected. We wonder whether this means certain characters will stick around longer than they were originally established in the actual-play Dungeons & Dragons campaign from which The Mighty Nein is adapted. Only time will tell.

The Mighty Nein airs exclusively on Prime Video. Season 1 is available to watch now, with season 2 set to debut on Mar. 24, 2027.

#3515. The Office's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

In 2005, two TV shows premiered as mid-season replacements, which isn't usually a great sign for said series' potential longevity. One was "Grey's Anatomy" on ABC, which became one of the longest-running TV shows in history. The other? "The Office," an adaptation of Ricky Gervais' British series of the same name that became one of the biggest hits in the entire history of NBC.

With Steve Carell leading the way as the well-meaning but unbelievably buffoonish Michael Scott (the regional manager of the Scranton branch of paper company Dunder-Mifflin), the American version of "The Office" made it past a somewhat rocky first season and became a small-screen staple, launching the careers of Carell and co-stars like John Krasinski, B.J. Novak, and Mindy Kaling. (It also, arguably, led to an uptick in small-screen mockumentaries like its successors "Modern Family," "Parks and Recreation," and "Abbott Elementary.") After running for nine massively successful seasons, "The Office" wrapped up its run in 2013 with a finale that actually stuck the landing ... but the road to the finish was rough.

You can argue all you want about how to pinpoint the downfall of "The Office," but I won't entertain any debate. The answer is that "The Office" hit a major point of no return in Season 7 when Carell left the show, which led to Michael Scott moving away from Scranton and decamping to Colorado. Despite its best efforts to continue relatively uninterrupted, the series just didn't functionally work without Michael Scott.

It's perfectly understandable that Steve Carell wanted to leave "The Office" behind after spending so long playing one character. (He's a pretty talented guy, after all.) Still, the show should have just ... ended. Even the lead-up to Michael's exit was, all things considered, sort of bleak. This is conjecture on my part, but it really felt like, in Season 6 episodes like "Scott's Tots" and "Koi Pond," the show was leaning into Michael's worst impulses and making him straight-up unlikable instead of silly but well-meaning.

The reason for Michael's departure, however, is undeniably sweet. After human resources representative Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) makes her debut appearance in the Season 4 finale "Goodbye Toby," she and Michael ultimately fall in love before she gets moved back to her original Dunder-Mifflin branch in Nashua due to higher-ups fretting about the pair's relationship. Then, in Season 7, she returns to Scranton, and while Holly and Michael have been broken up for some time when she finds herself back in northeastern Pennsylvania, they get back together ... but their happy ending is threatened when family troubles mean that Holly needs to move back to Colorado.

Thankfully, by this point in the series, Michael is back to being essentially likable again, so he does the right thing: He proposes to Holly and tells his colleagues he's moving with her. His final episode, "Goodbye Michael," is incredibly moving, especially the moment where Pam Beesly-Halpert (Jenna Fischer) says goodbye to Michael in the airport. Yet, the show loses its footing forever as he departs, and it never recovers. Why? Well, the string of potential replacements for Michael is lackluster at best and egregiously unfunny at worst.

One of the many crimes committed in the final two seasons of "The Office" is that the show managed to make English treasure and comedy legend Catherine Tate actively exhausting, but I'm getting ahead of myself. First, "The Office" pulls out the stops by bringing in Steve Carell's "Anchorman" cohort Will Ferrell (the proverbial comedic big gun) as Deangelo Vickers, a deeply confusing and unfunny new manager who's written off after getting a brain injury during a pickup basketball game. From there, Creed Bratton's erratic "Creed Bratton" briefly becomes the manager (and it goes just as well as any "Office" fan would expect), and while James Spader's unfathomably bizarre Robert California has his moments as one of Creed's successors, he doesn't work, either.

Ultimately, Tate's Nellie Bertram and Ed Helms' Andy Bernard are the people who run the Scranton branch most consistently in Michael's absence, and not only are they both terrible at the job, neither of them recreates the magic that only Carell could bring to the series. Instead, Tate's Nellie is, at varying times, exceedingly ridiculous or shrewd (it depends on the episode you're watching), whereas Andy is so expendable that "The Office" briefly writes him off. (This was done to free up Helms to go film "The Hangover Part III" at the time.) Moreover, everyone eventually gets simplified to the point of parody (i.e. Flanderized, to use a popular "Simpsons"-inspired term), so much so that Andy, himself an Ivy League graduate, becomes borderline illiterate. Put simply, it's a mess.

Yes, "The Office" has a great series finale, but the journey to getting there was rough without Michael Scott. Decide for yourself: The show is currently streaming on Peacock.

With the 2026 TV schedule heading into the holiday season, many are likely preparing for their favorite yuletide programming and getting ready for other festivities. We can reportedly count Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce amongst such people, as they are reportedly figuring out their first Christmas as a married couple. And apparently, deciding where to spend the holiday has become a little complicated. Per a new report, the newlyweds want to celebrate with both families without making either set of parents feel left out.

The Grammy winner and her Kansas City Chiefs tight end husband on married July 3 at Madison Square Garden, an event Kelce later described as one of the best nights of his life. Now, Rob Shuter alleges in his Naughty But Nice substack that the newlyweds have been discussing their first Christmas together. Per Shuter, an insider claims:

Neither wants to disappoint their parents, but they also don’t want their first Christmas as a married couple to become a tug-of-war. They want everyone to feel included.

It's a familiar holiday scheduling problem, although the families involved are rather more recognizable than most. Swift's parents, Andrea and Scott, have long been central to her Christmas celebrations, while Kelce remains close to his mother, Donna, and father, Ed. Swift even grew up on a Christmas tree farm in Pennsylvania, an experience she later turned into a holiday song. With both sets of traditions to consider, choosing where to spend the holiday allegedly hasn't been straightforward.

The Kelces already have some well-established food traditions. Kylie Kelce has praised Swift's baking alongside Donna Kelce's famous dinner rolls, so there would apparently be no shortage of people willing to contribute to Christmas dinner.

Also, the couple may already have a solution in mind. Instead of traveling between family gatherings or deciding which parents to visit, Shuter's sources says Swift and Kelce are considering hosting Christmas themselves. The idea would bring their relatives to one celebration, although no final plans have been publicly announced. A second source told Shuter:

They think bringing everyone together is the perfect answer. They get to start their own traditions without making either family feel they’ve lost out. It’s about creating one big family Christmas.

There's at least one reason a gathering away from a football stadium might be easier this year. As it so happens, the Chiefs don't have a game scheduled on Christmas Day in 2026, according to the team's published schedule. Kansas City is set to host the New England Patriots on Dec. 21 and the San Francisco 49ers on Dec. 27, leaving Christmas Day free of a game-day obligation.

Last Christmas looked a little different for the couple. The Chiefs played the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium on Dec. 25, with Swift and her parents in attendance. She and Kelce also surprised several stadium employees with Christmas gifts.

Kelce has already talked about looking forward to his first Christmas as a married man. Earlier this month, while promoting Tommy Hilfiger's winter collection, he told Women's Wear Daily he was excited to start new traditions with Swift. Although there's at least one he's apparently keeping: his mom Donna's homemade blueberry muffins.

The families have spent Christmas together before. Back in 2023, the “Shake it Off” performer's brother Austin showed up at a Chiefs game dressed as Santa Claus and surprised Kelce with a Christmas present. Both families also played a part in the couple's July wedding, with Austin serving as Swift's man of honor and Jason Kelce standing beside his brother as best man. The newlyweds even asked guests to make charitable donations instead of bringing wedding gifts. So, getting everyone together for Christmas wouldn't exactly be a first for the newlyweds.

Neither Swift nor Kelce has confirmed Shuter's report, so where they'll spend Christmas and whether both families will be there remains to be seen. But with the holiday just a few weeks away, they still have time to figure things out. However they end up celebrating, might I suggest checking out our list of the best Christmas movies? At least that'll give everyone something to watch once the presents are opened.

#3513. Kate Middleton Announces First Major Trip Since Her Cancer Diagnosis

In unexpected news, Kensington Palace has just announced that Kate Middleton will accompany Prince William on his upcoming three-day official visit to Mumbai, India. The trip, which commences on Monday, will mark their first joint tour outside the United Kingdom in the past four years and represents a new milestone in Kate Middleton’s gradual return to public duties since she was diagnosed with cancer in early 2024 and began scaling back her official engagements.

Last May, the princess made a brief solo trip to Italy to learn about early childhood development, but this trip to India (a nine-hour flight from London) represents her first long-distance journey and her highest-profile diplomatic engagement since the Caribbean tour she undertook in 2022 and the Earthshot Awards gala she attended in Boston that same year.

"So proud, I'm very, very proud. She's been amazing. She's been through so much in the last couple of years, particularly," William shared on UK radio show Heart Breakfast in May, pleased to see that Kate was “gradually resuming” her travels. Still, the heir to the throne wanted to be cautious and warned that these visits are very taxing. "Away trips like that take a lot out of you," he explained. "So we have to balance that, make sure she's, she's OK and rested, but she's in good form."

The royal couple at the 2022 Earthshot Prize ceremony in Boston, their most recent joint trip abroad to date

The reason for the visit is the sixth edition of the Earthshot Prize, an initiative spearheaded by the heir to the British throne that each year awards one million pounds (about $1,323,249) to five innovative environmental projects and which, after making stops in other cities abroad such as Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro, is now taking place in the country that has produced the most finalists and winners in the competition’s history.

Standout finalists this year include Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its fleet of electric motorcycle taxis designed to reduce urban pollution, and Mahila Housing Trust, which installs reflective roofs capable of lowering the temperature inside homes by up to five degrees during extreme heat. The awards ceremony will be held this Tuesday evening at the Jio World Centre in Mumbai and will feature a performance by the band Take That and be attended by celebrities such as actor Rami Malek.

William and Kate during their 2016 visit to the Taj Mahal

Hours before the main event, the Prince and Princess of Wales will also preside over the first edition of the Earthshot Children’s Awards, a competition in which 15,000 schools from 24 Indian states have participated with environmental proposals designed by young people aged 9 to 17. The itinerary also includes a solo appearance by Kate Middleton, meetings with the Bollywood film industry, cricket-related celebrations, and a possible meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In addition to being a positive sign regarding the princess’s health, this return to India holds strong symbolic significance for the couple, who last visited the country in April 2016. On that occasion, the then-Duke and Duchess of Cambridge visited the Taj Mahal and posed on the same white marble bench where Princess Diana was photographed alone in 1992—an image that has gone down in history as a reflection of the breakdown of her marriage to the now-King Charles III.

#3512. Robert Downey Jr.'s 90s Supernatural Fantasy Flop Is Worth Revisiting

It's no exaggeration to say that Ron Underwood's 1993 fantasy comedy film "Heart and Souls" boasts one of Robert Downey Jr.'s best performances. He wasn't nominated for an Oscar (although he surely deserved to be), but at least he won a Saturn Award for Best Actor for his work on it. Yet, because it flopped at the box office, it's rarely ranked among Downey's best movies of all time.

Downey stars in "Heart and Souls" as Thomas Reilly, an arrogant yuppie who is possessed by a pack of friendly ghosts that have been following him since birth. Thus, over the course of the movie, Downey takes on the speech patterns and affectations of his ghostly co-stars (Kyra Sedgwick, Tom Sizemore, Alfre Woodard, and Charles Grodin), and he does so with utter aplomb. The result is a film that's funny, profound, and sentimental in equal measure. It has the mood and structure of a high-concept Hollywood comedy, but with a toe rooted in the warmth of something like "It's a Wonderful Life." Plus, its view of the afterlife is pretty light and fun and makes sense in a secular way.

The world of ghosts plays by its own rules in "Heart and Souls," but it's not oblique or difficult. Here, the living and the dead are cosmically bound, like sometimes-invisible family members contracted to make wrongs right and assuage regrets. It's a positive and touching movie with its messages tucked in between hilarious bouts of Downey zaniness. Ultimately, Thomas learns to be less selfish and far more understanding to his girlfriend, Anne, played by Elisabeth Shue. See what I mean about the amazing cast?

"Heart and Souls" opens in 1959 and introduces us to our ghost characters while they're still alive, each of them boarding the same ill-fated bus. Julia (Kyra Sedgwick) is hoping to find her boyfriend, whose marriage proposal she regrets rejecting. Penny (Alfre Woodard) has to work a late shift away from her sons. Milo (Tom Sizemore) is a small-time crook who conned some valuable stamps from a local kid and regrets it. And Harrison (Charles Grodin) is a singer who just fled an audition due to overwhelming stage fright.

Sadly, their bus driver, Hal (David Paymer), gets distracted and crashes the vehicle, killing everyone on board in front of a car carrying a woman in labor. The four passengers, now ghosts, then witness a young Thomas being born. Over time, the ghosts realize they're physically bound to Thomas (meaning, they get dragged along if he walks away) and grow up with him. However, because they're invisible to everyone but him, Thomas' parents assume he's mentally unwell. So, the ghosts eventually decide to become invisible to Thomas to protect his mental health.

Fast-forward to the present, and the ghosts are unexpectedly visited by the now-deceased Hal. He tells them that Thomas is their "earthly vessel" and they should've been spending their time using him to right the wrongs in their lives so they can finally enter the afterlife. Now, they have to solve their biggest regrets in the next few days or risk oblivion.

Thomas, meanwhile, has become a heartless foreclosure banker who believes he had schizophrenia as a child, causing him to see his childhood "friends." But after the ghosts reappear to him, he eventually accepts that, yes, they are real, and he agrees to help them solve their earthly problems and ascend.

I maintain that "Heart and Souls" is one of the best films of its year. And, to reiterate, Robert Downey Jr. gives an Oscar-worthy performance in it. However, he wouldn't win his Oscar until "Oppenheimer" decades later, having only just been nominated for an Academy Award for the first time right before "Heart and Souls" came out for his turn as Charlie Chaplin in Richard Attenborough's biopic "Chaplin."

Overall, critics were mixed on "Heart and Souls." Most reviews tended to praise the performances from the movie's gaggle of stars, as seen in Michael Wilmington's review for the Los Angeles Times. He noted that "Heart and Souls" was about the spiritual crisis of modern humanity, "buried under several tons of Hollywood slick." But, he added, you should trust the film's actors. To quote him directly:

"There's one great opportunity for virtuoso fun here: the chance handed Downey to impersonate the mannerisms of his co-stars whenever one takes over his body. With [...] delicate, precise mimicry [...] he slips delightfully into [Alfre] Woodard's feline assurance, [Tom] Sizemore's swagger, [Kyra] Sedgwick's sexiness or [Charles] Grodin's repressions. The character he's playing — the same kind of languid, self-obsessed, inwardly anxious hedonist he played throughout the '80s — isn't deep, but Downey digs something comic out of his superficiality."

If that sounds fun or intriguing, it can serve as your "in" to "Heart and Souls." You may discover a new gem.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

Mormon Wives: Orange County doesn’t exactly live up to its name.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve ever watched The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, you know there’s no shortage of drama. Just look at Taylor Frankie Paul, who’s had a swingers scandal, the cancellation of her season of The Bachelorette, custody issues with her children, and chaos surrounding production. But the Hulu reality series was popular and created a lot of buzz, so I was not surprised when they announced the spinoff, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, currently on the 2026 TV schedule. However, the fact that it feels like the majority of the women in the new show are not Mormon and that some aren’t even wives is a bit weird and an interesting choice, considering the title, and viewers (including myself) have taken notice.

To catch you up in case you haven’t seen the original series, Jen Affleck, a 20-something Mormon wife and mother, joined MomTok in Utah to fight against the typical social norms and stereotypes that are common within the religion. After appearing in Season 34 of Dancing with the Stars as a celebrity contestant alongside fellow Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt, the mother of three with a fourth on the way decided to stay in Southern California, citing the fracturing of MomTok and the need for therapy to recover from everything that happened.

Seeming to instead have decided to jump right into another reality series, which again is an interesting choice, Jen has brought together a new group of friends, all of whom are mothers with their own drama and secrets, but who are not all Mormon, despite the show’s name. One has even admitted to signing on for the heightened visibility reality TV brings.

It’s hard not to notice that The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County is a cast divided into two groups, with the women who are Mormons being outnumbered by the women who are not. In the season premiere, cast member Aspyn Ovard (who's got a memorable storyline about being part of a throuple) says, “We’ve all been shaped by Mormonism in one way or another,” which is a bit of a vague statement when we don’t know all the details of the backgrounds of many of these women, and even she makes it clear that she’s very closed off to the church and its teachings.

I'm not the only one who has noticed this either, as this conversation has popped up all over social media, including places like Reddit, where fans have asked why non-Mormons are "even on the show." I get it's weird to call out someone's religious preferences, but when your show is called Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, I do think that leads to a certain expectation.

When you’re in the business of entertainment, building a franchise off of something successful and popular makes sense. But it’s hard to escape the weirdness of not really delivering on what your show’s title promises. All of this is not to say that the women who make up the OC spinoff cast don’t have compelling lives of their own, because they do, but the religious branding doesn’t entirely fit and feels like more of a subplot than a main focus, like it is in the original series.

And it all makes me wonder if the title should have just been something more reflective of Jen Affleck specifically? Just spitballing here.

For a reality show that’s supposed to be centered around Mormons, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County actually positions them to be the villains of the season. McCall DaPron, the older sister of the OG series’ Mayci Neeley, exhibits confrontational behavior. She gets into frequent clashes with other cast members, often leaving them to wonder whether it’s possible to keep this friend group together.

Her strong commitment to her faith and her efforts to share it with others, including best friend and co-star Jordan McClanahan (whom she successfully converted), rubs anyone not as devoted the wrong way. This is especially true when her need to influence others’ opinions and actions creates conflict.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives has had a seemingly endless amount of drama and scandals over four seasons, which are streaming with a Hulu subscription, but Mayci always came across like the most supportive one of the group on that show, where McCall seems less inclined to stay neutral. It’s hard to know how much of the drama is manipulated with editing, but it’s another interesting choice on a series that already seems to be trying to break its own formula.

All of this said, if there ends up being a second season of the OC spinoff, I will still definitely be tuning in!

Between Jen being pregnant with her fourth child at the same time she decides she wants a divorce, Aspyn trying to get her ex-husband to spend time with her current throuple, and Salomé Andrea figuring out if she can reconcile with a man she began dating in ninth grade and couldn’t marry in the Mormon church before she ultimately walked away from both, it is all definitely weird, but just weird enough to make me want to see what happens next.

#3509. Why Walter Koenig Held His Tongue To Keep His Star Trek II: The Wrath Of Khan Role

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" gives Pavel Chekov (the late Walter Koenig) one of his meatier arcs in any of the "Star Trek" films. In his new assignment as first officer of the USS Reliant, Chekov and his captain, Terrell (Paul Winfield), scout planets as a testing site for the Genesis device. But what they think is planet Ceti Alpha VI is actually the barren Ceti Alpha V, where the Enterprise left Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán), the 20th century's most infamous genetically engineered warlord, and his followers at the end of the episode "Space Seed."

Chekov and Terrell are captured and brainwashed via Ceti eels implanted in their ears. Khan and his people thus seize the Reliant, and boom, we have our movie. The sequence on Ceti Alpha V is predicated on Khan and Chekov recognizing each other. When Chekov and Terrell come across Khan and co.'s makeshift home, Chekov recognizes the name "Botany Bay" (the name of the sleeper ship where the Enterprise found Khan in "Space Seed"). Once the pair are captured, Khan recognizes Chekov and proclaims "I never forget a face."

Chekov also speaks to and of Khan as if he witnessed the events of "Space Seed." Except, technically, he didn't. "Space Seed" was made in "Star Trek" Season 1, and Koenig/Chekov only joined the cast in Season 2. Ergo, he obviously never appeared in "Space Seed" and shared no screentime with Khan. Oops!

Over 40 years later, Trekkies still note the inconsistency and rationalize it. Koenig, for his part, has said he recognized the error when he read the script, but chose to stay silent to preserve Chekov's role. Considering how often "Star Trek" overlooked Chekov, it's hard to blame him.

"Wrath of Khan" writer Harve Bennett wasn't a "Star Trek" fan when he took the job. That worked for the best. "Wrath of Khan" is widely credited for revitalizing "Star Trek" and part of that is because Bennett and director Nicholas Meyer brought fresh eyes. To that end, they couldn't expect everyone who would go see "Wrath of Khan" had previously seen "Space Seed." So, the movie doesn't rely on the episode outside of its big picture story details, which are easily explained via some dialogue in Khan's first scene. (I saw "Wrath of Khan" before "Space Seed" as a kid, and I followed the former just fine.)

But Chekov knowing Khan is the kind of detail that evidently slipped by Bennett. Koenig, who was asked to read the script and give it a "Trekkie read," had a vested interest in not pointing out the mistake. As Koenig put it when interviewed in "The Fifty-Year Mission: The First 25 Years" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman: "I was faced with the ethical dilemma of mentioning it to Bennett or letting it go. I chose survival as opposed to ethics."

Chekov is the only member of the "Star Trek" main cast who shares physical screentime with Khan in the movie. (Khan and Kirk only ever talk via viewscreens and communicators.) It's also Khan's first appearance in the movie, as well as the scene from "Wrath of Khan" that I rewatch the most in isolation. Montalbán's performance, savoring every line, is just spectacular. I can see why Koenig would, as an actor, want the chance to be in a scene as strong as that one, and he holds his own balancing Chekov's courage and fear.

For Koenig's part, his cheeky theory to explain away this inconsistency was that Chekov once made Khan wait an uncomfortable amount of time to use the Enterprise's restroom. "Chekov was on the Enterprise, just offscreen" has become the go-to fanon answer. The novel "To Reign in Hell: The Exile of Khan Noonien Singh" by Greg Cox legitimizes that; Chekov is said to have led a failed effort to retake the Enterprise from Khan, and is part of the detachment that helps Khan and his people get settled on Ceti Alpha V.

Despite the continuity gap with "Space Seed," Chekov was the best pick among the main characters as the one captured by Khan. Amusingly, this is precisely because he's the most ancillary one. The Enterprise can function without him in a way it wouldn't without Spock (Leonard Nimoy) or Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley).

While Koenig evidently feared that they would swap Chekov's part out in the script, the only other main character who could work would be Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), which would add some icky subtext to Khan violating her body with the Ceti eels, or Sulu (George Takei). With Sulu, you run into the same problem because he wasn't in "Space Seed" either! While Sulu/Takei was part of the show in Season 1, he was absent for that particular episode. If it had been Sulu who landed on Ceti Alpha V with Terrell and met Khan, you might be getting forum posts highlighting that inconsistency today.

Walter Koenig may have created a small problem in "Wrath of Khan" by staying silent here, but he helped fix a much bigger one, too, by suggesting moving Spock's death to the end of the film.

#3508. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

In Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, the director follows the rise of OpenAI and a few of its pioneers: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati. The result is one of the most talked-about and timely films of the season.

“The topic is not the artificial intelligence for me, but it's the people who imagined it, who created it, who exploited it and who are still in the mix of doing all these things,” Guadagnino said during a discussion led by VF's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, at Vanity Fair’s Screening Room at LACMA on Saturday. “I was very much into trying to decipher, understand this world of this new generation, let’s say tech bros, that were somehow behaving in a way that was not exactly as you could see the previous generation doing … So it was too attractive not to try to meet these people in the eyes and too attractive not to do so with this incredible group of performers who were going to go and jump the cliff of this.”

Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation. The actors were challenged with preparing to play real people who they were not able to interact with ahead of time, instead relying on interviews, video recordings, and other research in order to get into their characters.

Andrew Garfield at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

“[Sam Altman] still is unknowable to me and I'm fascinated by him continuously and exponentially, for here until eternity," Garfield said about OpenAI's co-founder and CEO. “And it's important to try to understand because as Luca said, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. He added: “It's a remarkable thing to have the resilience to go and sleep every night, knowing that you're really doing a lot of damage.”

Barbaro said the fact that Murati is very private helped her understand the former OpenAI CTO. “That is indicative of a kind of behavior and personality type and it pointed me in a certain direction as far as her values were concerned,” she said. “And we also had a lot of wonderful consultants, people who worked with them at OpenAI, but who were no longer with the company, kind of telling us what jokes and things that they would make.”

Yura Borisov at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

For Borisov, he hopes his portrayal does Sutskever justice and that people will want to know or understand him more. “I started to watch videos about him and looked at his social media, trying just to understand what he's talking about in his interviews,” the actor explained. "And step by step, as much as I discovered him, it was more and more scary for me because I started to respect and love him more and more."

Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

The conversation had its own meta moment of sorts, when Barbaro posed a question to Guiducci about his decision to profile and feature Altman on the cover of Vanity Fair’s New Establishment Issue.

"You faced heat for presenting, maybe some people would say pedestalizing Sam Altman on the cover of Vanity Fair, what is your take on that?" Barbaro asked.

“I think that the magazine is an arena where these things have to play out,” Guiducci said. “It's so interesting to me to...have the [forthcoming] feature about this film in the issue that was preceded by one where I got to ask Sam about it." Guiducci continued: "Something about [taking Sam's] picture makes people feel, ‘Oh, that's the trophy.’ But photojournalism is journalism too. And I want people to be able to look back at the magazine and see a document of the time that we lived in," he said. "And also, if the photo is what helps me get the interview where we get to know more about these people, I'm going to take it.”

Monica Barbaro at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Other panel highlights included the subject of ChatGPT, which only Guadagnino admitted to using occasionally to ask about what’s ok to feed his dogs. He also addressed parting ways with the film's original studio partner Amazon and the fortuitous partnership that emerged with new distributor NEON.

“I think there is some kind of honor in the decision because they could have written off the movie and that's it,” he said about Amazon dropping the film from their slate. “And then they allowed us to find a partner and we found the best partner possible… They really believed in the movie.”

“They really made everything to get us to make the best movie we could,” he continued. "I only have good feelings toward my friends at Amazon. And in a strange way, I kind of understand the decision. Conflict of interest is a big thing.”

Luca Guadagnino at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026
