#3490. Xbox Head of Next Gen Finally Explains What Project Helix Is: ‘It Is Not a PC’

Xbox wants Project Helix to have access to a unified games library

To celebrate 25 years of Xbox, the company released a special publication that let fans look back at its past and glimpse its plans for the future. The digital magazine features a conversation with Jason Ronald, Xbox Vice President of Next Generation, who provides an inside look into the creation of Project Helix, Xbox's next-gen console.

Ronald underlined that game preservation is a key element in the creation of Project Helix. As he sees it, owning a new console doesn't mean you have to leave behind your previous-gen games. Therefore, it's important to ensure that Project Helix is backward compatible with all previous Xbox consoles, allowing fans to continue to have access to and play their games. This way, game libraries will move alongside players wherever they go, rather than being left behind.

Nowadays, it's not as common for players to stick to a single platform, which is why games across all platforms are being taken into consideration. Xbox wants to break barriers and give players access to a unified gaming library. Ronald says that "Helix is a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games." The goal is to make it easy and intuitive, whether you're a "hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options."

To make this happen, Xbox is taking inspiration from ROG Ally and Xbox Mode, both of which were steps in the direction that Xbox is headed. It seems that access to a unified games' library, multiple storefronts, portability, and PC-like navigation are all features Xbox would like to include in its next-gen console. Feedback on the ROG Ally has played a big role in creating a prototype for Project Helix.

"The feedback that we've gotten from players has fundamentally informed and altered our plans for how [a unified library] actually shows up in a future console. Players shared where we met the mark and areas we needed to improve or approach differently. So absolutely, we view the Ally as a precursor to what we're doing with Helix."

Xbox wants to put "players at the center" in its next generation of consoles, and building Project Helix around feedback is certainly one way of doing it. There is one important question that remains on fans' minds: will Project Helix have a disc drive?

If being able to play games from each generation is such a crucial focal point for Xbox, then being able to use discs should go beyond the disc-to-digital program. While game digitization is a great option to have, it is limited to Xbox One and Series X/S consoles and still only leaves players with a digital license, which is not equivalent to game ownership.

Affordability is another major consideration in the creation of Project Helix. While console gaming used to be an affordable entry point into the world of video games, the component crisis has definitely changed this.

"It's definitely a challenging time, but as a system and a platform designer, it's also one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable."

It seems that Xbox is working hard to find a way around these hurdles to deliver the best product it can. Adding a disc drive would likely conflict with the system's affordability, but it would certainly win points with fans disgruntled by the imminent all-digital future.

#3489. Casting Walter White: How ‘Breaking Bad’ Found Bryan Cranston

While the Breaking Bad universe would eventually expand to include dozens of characters, the pilot was actually a tidy affair. At its center was Walter White, whose journey would require an actor of extraordinary depth and nuance. It’s not an exaggeration to say that the success or failure of Breaking Bad would rest primarily on his sagging shoulders.

SHARON BIALY, casting director: I don’t know if Bryan knows this, but when Sherry [Bialy] and I went in to meet with Vince to try to get the job as casting directors—­our “audition”—­we literally said, “You may think we’re crazy. We hope you don’t fire us before you hire us. But what about Bryan Cranston?” And he said, “By golly, that’s who I want. I worked with him on The X-­ Files.”

Sherry and I did a lot of theater at the time. We were doing Aaron Sorkin’s new play [The Farnsworth Invention], and Bryan came in and read. We were blown away. He was so talented on Malcolm in the Middle, obviously, but this was live theater with a lot of language. Anyway, Bryan didn’t get the role, but his audition was incredible. And I never forgot it.

VINCE GILLIGAN, creator: Bryan was the only guy I was thinking of when I wrote the script. I had written an episode of The X-­ Files called “Drive,” which came out in 1998, and I was lucky enough to hire him to play the bad guy.

We were really struggling to cast this role because we needed a guy who could be really scary, someone who could make us feel like our hero, Agent Mulder, could get his head blown off at any second. But also, he had to be kind of an asshole. [Throughout the episode] he’s ranting about the government. He’s ranting about stuff like, “Agent Mulder— is that a Jewish name?”

He’s a thoroughly unlikable guy. And yet you had to feel bad for him, for what happens to him at the end of the episode. You had to feel sympathy.

We only had a day or two left before production was going to start. We were going to have to settle on somebody. We had plenty of actors come in who were scary as all get out, but they weren’t necessarily likable. And then this guy walks in the door: Bryan Cranston. Never heard of him before. And he nails it in the audition. As he left, we all stood up and shook his hand, and then I looked to the other producers and to Rick Millikan, our casting director, and I said, “Off to wardrobe!” He was that good.

When I came up with the idea of Breaking Bad, I thought, This is a guy who, again, is going to be very unlikable. He’s going to do a lot of unlikable things, and the audience still has to sympathize with him. Who would be good for this role? I know! That guy, Bryan Cranston. And I wrote it for him. I never really had anyone else in mind.

MELISSA BERNSTEIN, co-executive producer: He was in an episode of X-­Files, playing this racist, and somehow, over the course of the episode, you go from loathing him to feeling badly that he doesn’t make it. He just was able to make someone so unsavory be human. Vince also said, “And he’s so great with comedy. I just feel it in my bones that he could bring those chops to drama—­his sense of timing, the way he embodies those choices physically. He’s perfect.”

BRYAN CRANSTON: I instruct young actors all the time that without a healthy dose of luck, you will not have a career. And this [episode of The X-­ Files] was a lucky break for me.

I had just gotten back from shooting this little movie that I wrote and directed, called Last Chance. I spent all of our money on it, and by the end I was like, Wow, what are we doing on this film? But we rolled the dice on it, and now I was back in town and got a call from my agent about an audition. I said, “Whatever it is, let me know, because I really could use the money.” It just so happened that my look at the time, from this movie that I did, was a perfect look for this guy [on The X-­Files]. So, I went in, and I got the job—­and I was grateful for it.

It’s only in retrospect that I realized Vince Gilligan wanted to see me [to discuss Breaking Bad] was because I had played this reprehensible character that, despite his actions, still needed the audience to root for his life. Despite the despicable person in the back seat, David Du­chovny’s humanity would not allow him to just pull over and say, “Fuck it, die. You’re a horrible human being. I just want you to die.” He couldn’t do it. That’s really, in a nutshell, what Vince Gilligan does.

I knew intuitively that coming off seven years of a comedy, I needed to look for a drama. If I didn’t, I could have been typecast. If you want to expand on the opportunities that may present themselves, you need to take control. I was offered a couple of comedy pilots that I turned down, and I was perfectly willing to wait. Then Breaking Bad came into my lap.

I read it . . . and I couldn’t believe it. I was stunned. I thought, This is perhaps the best hour­-long screenplay that I’ve ever read. I felt tremendous empathy for this character. This poor guy who is just struggling. And I was the same age as Walter White—­I was fifty.

But reading the pilot, I didn’t know where it was going. You have this fish­ out­ of­ water teacher, cooking crystal meth? How could that possibly be sustained year after year after year? How can someone who knows nothing about that world survive? And Vince explained that he wanted to turn Mr. Chips into Scarface.

In the same way that The Sopranos is unthinkable with someone other than James Gandolfini in the role of Tony Soprano, I can’t get my head around the idea of a version of Breaking Bad that doesn’t include Bryan Cranston. But this is Hollywood, and even on basic cable, you don’t just sign up a former sitcom star—­ not even one as gifted as Bryan—­and hand him the starring role in a complex drama without a bit of, shall we say . . . discussion.

MARK JOHNSON, executive producer: Obviously, some people came up for Walter White who were names, but we never got around to entertaining them seriously. It was Vince’s idea to cast him. And despite the fact that there wasn’t a unanimous wave of approval, there wasn’t the kind of pushback that you’d probably have today, in large part because I don’t think the expectation was that we were going to get any real name, any big name.

MELISSA BERNSTEIN: AMC had found Jon Hamm for Mad Men, and they sort of got to reintroduce him to the business. I think they thought we would do something similar with Bryan.

CHARLIE COLLIER, president, general manager, AMC: I was never in the room when they were debating the cast with Vince and Mark. That would have been the programming group. And then they would come back to us and say, “They want that father from Malcolm in the Middle.” And we’d be like, “Really? He’s going to be the linchpin for this whole ambitious project?”

CHRISTINA WAYNE, senior VP, scripted programming, AMC: When Vince suggested Bryan, we all kind of said, “That guy from Malcolm in the Middle?” And then he started showing us a bunch of tape of Bryan in other things, and I was, like, Oh my God—­he’s a total chameleon.

JAMIE ERLICHT, co­-president, Sony Pictures Television: It’s funny. This is one of those great Hollywood stories that has been told so many times. You sit on the sidelines and watch, and it takes on a life of its own. That life is a little different than the truth, sure, but it’s a better story.

The story is that Zack [Van Amburg] and I heard “Bryan Cranston,” and we were really unsure, and we tried to convince Vince that, No, that’s not the way to go. That’s part of a story about how despite all the forces against him, Bryan Cranston became Walter White.

It’s a great story. I love that story. I mean, I don’t love that story.

The truth is, the show was going forward. We weren’t worried about the writing because Vince was knocking it out of the park. The directing? We weren’t worried about the directing. The casting was going to be the next critical element. If you don’t have it—­ well, it’s funny to think about it now. With ninety­ nine point nine percent of other actors in that role, that show is just a well­ written good show that doesn’t become the legacy show that it’s become. And so Vince brought up Bryan Cranston.

I had worked with Bryan on King of Queens. He was the wacky neighbor, a guest star. I was a mid­ level executive, and I was in charge of that show. I always thought he brought a lot of comedic value, just like he did on Seinfeld, and obviously Malcolm in the Middle.

So, when the name Bryan Cranston came up, I was like, Hmmm, that’s interesting. I’ve never seen him do the more dramatic stuff. Do you think he can do it?

Vince was very passionate. He said he had worked with him on X-­Files, and that’s where he really saw what he was capable of on the drama side. We said, “Great, would you send us the X-­Files episode?” Which he did. I remember it was the next day. Zack and I were watching it. We looked at each other and said, “It’s a little bit of a leap of faith, but Vince is passionate, and Bryan is truly talented. Sure, we’re in.” The process took all of thirty­ six hours.

That version of the story, the true version of the story, is not as sexy as the one where Bryan jumped through thirty­ nine hoops and almost didn’t get cast. But that’s how it happened.

ZACK VAN AMBURG, co­-president, Sony Pictures Television: Remember, at this point, Michael Chiklis had gone from doing comedy to being a badass antihero (in The Shield). So, on one hand, you worry: Wait, are we just pulling a page out of the same playbook? Let’s take another sitcom guy and have him do a dark drama.

I think Vince was really clear on why he wanted Bryan. There was a likability factor that was undeniable. There was also a sort of sympathy that Bryan was able to elicit. And Vince also said, “No, wait a second—­ this guy’s also a dramatic actor.”

While some of this stuff gets lost in the haze of time—­ and the internet has a way of transforming rumors into something disguised as fact—­ it’s fair to say that Bryan was always the first choice for the role of Walter White. Regardless of what you may have heard, no one else was offered the job. Not Matthew Broderick, not John Cusack. No one. But you can’t fault anyone for doing their due diligence.

SHARON BIALY: The network likes names. They want to talk about other names. We did that. We did a couple of auditions and meetings. We just met recently with an actor on something else, and he reminded me that he was in the waiting room when Bryan walked out, and he turned to the other three actors and said, “We should all just go home. It’s over. That guy’s going to get it.”

VINCE GILLIGAN: We saw a lot of really good actors, several of them now famous names. They never dissuaded me that Bryan was the guy. And luckily, Bryan said yes, because he was up at the same time for a pilot for Fox that was going to pay him . . . well, my understanding is, substantially more money. Like a doctor show. Thank goodness he went with us instead.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3487. Star Trek: Picard Started As A Pitch For An Underused Original Series Character

Over the course of its three-season run, "Star Trek: Picard" took viewers along for the final voyage of the legendary Starfleet captain played by the equally legendary Patrick Stewart. But while the series was heavily rooted in Picard's history, referenced storylines in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and even spent its final season giving us the "TNG" crew getting back together for one last ride that viewers really wanted all along, the original idea for the show was apparently very different.

According to an interview with Trekcore, "Picard" co-creators Alex Kurtzman and Kristen Beyer started out with an idea that would've featured another character from the "Star Trek" universe that arguably deserved the spotlight even more than the famous captain: Nyota Uhura, the groundbreaking communications officer of the original "Enterprise," originally played by Nichelle Nichols.

Early in the development of what would eventually become "Picard," Beyer and Kurtzman started with the idea of bringing Nichols back to play her iconic role for the first time since 1991. Beyer recalled the initial idea:

"We were actually beginning with an Uhura story, and the idea was that we very much wanted to see we could bring Nichelle [Nichols] back in at this point in time, and then see what kind of stories [Uhura] might tie in to. And then Patrick's name came into the mix, and could we get him, would he be interested ... so the very first idea was a meeting between Uhura and Picard — a very, very young Picard."

Kurtzman gave a few more details about the idea, indicating that at one point, Uhura's role may have been more of a cameo than as the driving force of the show:

"The original idea was that a young Picard had been called to a hospital where Uhura had a mission for him, and it was related to the Borg."

It's an intriguing idea for a lot of reasons. From a real world perspective, it would've rectified a glaring oversight in how Nichols' legacy has been overlooked. Despite the fact that her portrayal of Uhura, which featured television's first interracial kiss between Nichols and costar William Shatner, was praised by no less than Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and inspired real-life astronaut Mae Jemison, among others, Uhura was extremely underused in the original series, even having her scenes rewritten to minimize her role. She's also the only member of the original series' bridge crew to never return for another appearance after "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country." Nichols was offered and turned down a small cameo role on "Star Trek: Voyager," but sadly, since she passed away in 2022, her return will always be something fans never get to see.

There are also a lot of fascinating questions from the nerdier in-universe view as well. Considering that "Star Trek: The Next Generation" takes place nearly 100 years after the events of the original series, any meeting between Uhura and Picard might seem pretty unlikely. That said, "Star Trek" has always found a way to keep its classic characters in circulation, whether it was through the transporter trickery that allowed Scotty (James Doohan) to come back in the "TNG" episode "Relics," the extended Vulcan lifespan that saw Spock still traveling the universe well into his second century, or just the extended lifespan of the utopian future that gave us a 137-year-old Dr. McCoy wandering around the "Enterprise-D" in the pilot episode of "TNG."

The bigger question is about the Borg, who did wind up being a major element of "Picard." They were a completely unknown species when the "Enterprise" first encountered them in the second season of "TNG," so Uhura knowing about them well before Picard took command of the Federation flagship, and telling him about them, is certainly a surprising development. Then again, the Borg are no strangers to time travel. It's entirely possible that Uhura's long career in Starfleet could've seen her encounter them, even if she probably should've given everyone else a heads up before all that stuff where they captured Picard and then blew up half the fleet. The Borg may have given us some of the best moments in "Trek," but a warning could've saved the Federation a lot of trouble

We're also left wondering whether this meeting between Uhura and a young Picard would've been a prelude to Patrick Stewart's return, or if we'd have seen another actor taking over the role, much like Celia Rose Gooding did with the role of Uhura herself on "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds." There are a couple of obvious choices for the role, of course, but it seems unlikely that they could've gotten Tom Hardy (who played Picard's younger clone Shinzon in "Star Trek: Nemesis"), and that kid who played a young Picard in the "TNG" episode "Rascals" has to be pushing 50 by now. Sadly, we'll never know.

Bowen Yang made a surprise cameo on Saturday Night Live this past weekend. The beloved former cast member appeared in multiple sketches, first as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the cold open and later as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in John Mulaney’s wild musical number about New York City. Yang seemed comfortable and back in his element, but it turns out the behind the scenes wasn’t exactly smooth sailing. Sarah Sherman actually had to fill in for him during dress rehearsal, leading to a hilarious visual that’s making the rounds.

Yang is currently crushing it as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway production of Oh, Mary! His schedule on the show, however, isn’t exactly SNL friendly. The Lyceum Theatre offers two performances every Saturday: one at 5 PM and one at 8:30 PM. Since SNL’s dress rehearsal starts at 8 PM, there was no way for the actor to appear in both; so, during the cold open, Sarah Sherman appeared in Yang’s part, hilariously wearing a sign that said Bowen Yang. According to Late Nighter, Marcello Hernández warned the crowd ahead of time, though I can’t imagine they expected this visual, which Yang later posted to his Instagram account…

A post shared by Bowen Yang (@fayedunaway)

It’s unclear exactly when the details of Yang’s appearance came together, but he reportedly did head to Studio 8H after his Broadway show on Friday to do a rehearsal for his two scenes. I can’t imagine longtime showrunner Lorne Michaels would be okay with a random celebrity doing a cameo without the standard rehearsing schedule, but he obviously knows Bowen well enough to know he didn’t need the full runthrough.

He clearly didn’t either, as he was a standout during the live show in both the cold open and as Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel in the musical number. Saidah Belo-Osagie reportedly played the second part very capably during the dress rehearsal, but that was never going to work for the live show. She had another role in the sketch, and also, Mary Todd Lincoln Tunnel was clearly written for Yang, as he’s currently playing Mary Todd Lincoln in the aforementioned show. He probably would have been personally offended if he wasn’t asked and tuned into SNL to see someone else doing an outrageous take on the part he’s currently playing on Broadway.

We’ve gotten two consecutive weeks with cameos from former cast members, as Bobby Moynihan appeared in the Davis S Pumpkins anniversary sketch and in a segment on Weekend Update as Drunk Uncle. Personally, I’d love to see SNL try and do double appearances more often. It’s always fun to see old favorites surprise fans by appearing in a sketch, but it’s even more fun to see those familiar faces show up twice during the same episode so they have a little more to do.

SNL is currently on hiatus for a few weeks, but it’ll return in early December with a new episode hosted by Amanda Seyfried. I cannot wait, as she should bring something new and exciting to 30 Rock and will hopefully continue the momentum as the show has recently dropped its strongest episodes of the season, including this past weekend's heater where John Mulaney brought some of the sharpest social commentary we've gotten in a long time.

#3485. As MAGA Melts Down, MAHA Is Also Breaking Apart—Starting With the Moms

In August 2024, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suspended his presidential campaign and endorsed Donald Trump, bringing his ragtag bunch of supporters—crunchy mamas, anti-vaxxers, and conspiracy theorists; testosterone bros, peptide enthusiasts, and people who put a “COEXIST” bumper sticker on their car in the 1990s—along for the ride. But now that the blue wave or tsunami—pick your tortured water metaphor—has come to pass, the fractures within MAHA threaten to break the movement apart, driven by bitter disappointment with the Trump administration.

“I think we are seeing a fracturing of the MAHA movement as those concerns start pulling people in different directions,” says Sandro Galea, dean of the Bursky School of Public Health at Washington University in St. Louis. Groups that are interested in healthier food are not necessarily the same as groups opposed to vaccines, he points out; it’s not a sure thing that those groups will continue to find common cause.

The crack-up didn’t start with the midterms, though the fact that most MAHA-backed candidates lost certainly accelerated it. Earlier this year, Trump had to withdraw his nomination of MAHA darling Casey Means for surgeon general after her stance on vaccines made it impossible for Republicans to get enough votes to support her confirmation. In May, MAHA ally Marty Makary, the commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, resigned, reportedly because of pressure from the administration to authorize fruit-flavored vapes. And in October, Calley Means—Casey’s brother—resigned from his high-level post under Secretary Kennedy at Health and Human Services, with MAHA outrage on unmet promises growing.

Three days after the midterms, Joe Rogan released a bomb-throwing, names-naming, two-plus-hour interview with Calley Means, in which the former Kennedy adviser used the word “demonic,” possibly in the literal sense, eight times.

The big takeaway was that Susie Wiles seemed to have told Kennedy to go sit in a corner and play by himself. All roads to Trump went through her office, and according to Means, she slow-walked, watered down, or outright quashed many MAHA priorities. According to Means, she did this primarily because of her and her family’s financial ties to lobbying on behalf of big business.

Wiles did not respond to a request for comment, but a spokesperson for Wiles previously told Axios that these allegations were “outrageous, defamatory, and provably false.”

Means argued that MAHA managed some wins: Trump signed an executive order to boost research on the use of psychedelics for treating mental health conditions. The new food pyramid instructs Americans to eat more steak than oatmeal. (In this economy?) There have been other MAHA victories too: The administration made it easier for Americans to get a handful of unproven injectable peptides, including the “Wolverine stack.” Trump signed an executive order in support of regenerative farming. The administration requested changes to the labels on testosterone products in an effort to make the hormone easier to prescribe—good news for Pete Hegseth’s promise of a “high-T Department of War.” It asked food manufacturers to voluntarily phase out some food dyes. It has sought to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines.

Means did not cite the United States recently losing its measles-elimination status as a win, though that was also a result of MAHA talking points.

The MAGA-MAHA mind meld provided plenty for the wellness bros, but precious little of what MAHA moms were expecting from their alliance with Trump. Tiffany Cianci, a high-profile MAHA advocate who goes by @thevinomom on Instagram, says the results were “small things,” not the massive systemic changes that had been promised.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for HHS pushed back on this narrative, writing, in part, “HHS has delivered the most sweeping public health reforms in modern history…Across the federal government, the administration has transformed food and nutrition policy, invested more than $1 billion in regenerative agriculture and farm modernization, and taken action to address harmful chemical exposures.”

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. delivers remarks during an event at HHS in August. The event highlighted a series of 'landmark actions' to improve the nation's food.

For the MAHA moms, there are two original sins of Trump 2.0. The first is the administration’s outright support for glyphosate, an herbicide that has been classified as a probable carcinogen by a World Health Organization agency. The second is its failure to put out a definition of ultra-processed foods, which the movement sees as the first step toward curbing those foods, particularly in school lunches. One was never released; Means alleged to Rogan that ultra-processed-food initiatives such as this were stymied by White House officials including Wiles, who he said told him, “I need sugar money.” Reporting found that food CEOs leaned on the White House to make the definition go away.

A White House official said on background that the definition for ultra-processed food remains a priority and is actively being worked on by relevant agencies. White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said that “the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump…The administration has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

However, the Trump administration has arguably hindered research on ultra-processed foods in other ways. A leading scientist who was studying ultra-processed food’s link to diabetes and obesity took early retirement from the National Institutes of Health last year after NIH officials, he said, censored the reporting of some of his study results because the study didn’t prove the hypothesis of ultra-processed-food addiction as they had hoped it would. If he’s to be believed, one of our best hopes for understanding the health risks of ultra-processed foods exited due to the actions of MAHA officials. (Vanity Fair has reached out to HHS for comment on the allegations of censorship; an HHS spokesperson previously told The New York Times, “NIH scientists have, and will, continue to conduct interviews regarding their research through written responses or other means. We remain committed to promoting gold-standard research and advancing public health priorities.”)

“We do have a food supply that’s nearly 70% ultra-processed food,” says Jessica Knurick, a registered dietitian and science communicator on social media. She counters that many of MAHA’s alleged priorities are aligned with the hopes of public health workers and nutritionists—yet the movement writ large has eroded trust in the very professionals who do that work. “They really want fewer environmental toxins. If you want that, you need strong regulation on corporations,” she says. “They voted in an administration that is decisively deregulatory.”

“All of the things that the MAHA movement claimed to have wanted,” she adds, “this administration has legislated in the exact opposite direction.”

See, for instance, the glyphosate debacle. Instead of curbing the herbicide, something for which he’d long been an advocate, Kennedy got on board with Trump’s support of it, including an executive order that actually prioritized production of the chemical under the bizarre guise of national security. Then the administration supported Roundup weed killer manufacturer Monsanto, now owned by Bayer, in a case before the Supreme Court, which resulted in a decision shielding the company from state-level lawsuits brought by those who believed they’d been harmed by the glyphosate-containing product. (Glyphosate-based Roundup products are no longer produced for the US residential market.)

This flew in the face of everything MAHA believed about Kennedy’s priorities. Vani Hari, a MAHA influencer who goes by the Food Babe, has been called both the Jenny McCarthy of food and a Democratic infiltrator. She thinks that the last nearly two years resulted in some positive change. She also tells me that she’s become somewhat disillusioned: “There have also been deeply disappointing decisions, particularly when it comes to glyphosate and pesticides.”

Despite it all, the HHS secretary continues to be deified by the vast majority of MAHA leaders, who don’t blame Kennedy for these setbacks. Cianci, however, blames just about everyone involved. “What I see within MAHA right now is a fracturing into one very, very small sliver that loves the proximity to power and the fundraising. They unfortunately tied their hitch to the wrong horse, which is partisanship,” she says. “And you have the rest of us that actually want our kids to be healthy.”

Supporters of the Make America Healthy Again movement are seen at a news conference on removing synthetic dyes from America's food supply, at the Health and Human Services Headquarters in Washington, DC, 2025.

If there is a road forward for MAHA, it might be best exemplified by Elizabeth Frost, a community health advocate and the leader of MAHA Ohio. She comes by her skepticism of the pharmaceutical industry honestly, after growing up in Appalachian Ohio during the height of the opioid epidemic. She now runs a political consultancy in the state, which she says works with both parties.

Beginning last year, Frost partnered with epidemiologists from Yale to find out how the people of East Palestine, Ohio, were still being affected by toxic exposures after the 2023 derailment of a train filled with hazardous materials. Frost went to bat for the scientists, lending her local grassroots credibility to their study on water quality in the town.

“I think there is a broader anti-corporate movement in America that hasn’t really been given a home with either established party because both parties have their own pet corporate interests,” she tells me. After Kennedy’s ascent, she had hoped for a focus on the MAHA issues that enjoy broad support. “Vaccines are not the most popular issue even for MAHA. Most people in MAHA would prefer for the majority of time to be spent talking about issues that are a little bit more unifying”—rather than something like Steak ’n Shake’s now using beef tallow for its french fries. “It’s just not where people’s hearts are.”

Speaking of no heart: Stephen Miller has been promoted to chief of staff after Wiles was forced out in the wake of the midterms. Both Calley Means and Secretary Kennedy have celebrated the move. “Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken,” Kennedy wrote on X.

But some MAHA moms are not so sure about the kraken. Cianci says that within MAHA, “people are very, very, very uncomfortable” with Miller. “If you’re just going to do what you’ve been told to do and take it to the extreme—he’s like the human embodiment of the paper clip problem,” she says.

Frost is similarly concerned about how things might go under Miller. “I don’t expect that on environmental exposures, industrial contamination, a strong streak against corporate influence—I doubt we’re going to get those things,” she says. She is also dismayed by MAHA leadership’s embrace of convicted rapist Russell Brand. “What the hell are we doing?” she wonders.

A person familiar with MAHA thinking who spoke on background counters that while it’s fair to say that Miller might be polarizing, he is also not beholden to corporate interests the way Wiles was, making him far less likely to block the scrutiny of pesticides and healthy food policies.

Cianci, Frost, and Hari all hope that MAHA will survive by focusing on policy over partisanship. “I also believe MAHA’s future must be bipartisan,” Hari wrote in an email.

Cianci sees opposition to data centers as the next big issue on which MAHA can lead. And she hopes that the anti-corporate tilt she sees in MAHA will spread. “We had a record number of candidates get elected to Congress this year that turned down all corporate PAC money. That is indicative of the MAHA movement. That is indicative of anti-corruption. And I think they’re going hand in glove.”

Frost would like to see Republicans work with progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on shared goals, like getting pesticides out of the food supply. She wants legislators to realize that “the way to hold their seat is to work across aisles on issues that their constituents care about.”

Perhaps MAHA can reinvent itself by leveraging some of its most popular issues to make common cause with Democrats. After all, 30% of midterm voters told pollsters that they support the MAHA movement, while many more—the vast majority of Americans—say that food additives and pesticide use should be more regulated. A plurality of Americans do not want data centers in their communities. The movement’s best hope for staying relevant is probably the (currently very pissed) MAHA moms, whose concerns about food and pollution were always the most broadly resonant parts of the MAHA platform—rather than a yen for peptides, beef tallow, or testosterone.

Most people want to be able to afford healthy food and effective health care. Trump’s rule has not made those things more accessible, with high cost of living, massive cuts to Medicaid, the ending of certain Affordable Care Act subsidies, and reductions in federal funding for SNAP benefits.

The challenge with a rebrand is that the connection to MAGA is right there in the name. But Trump’s presidency clearly has a shelf life, and MAHA wants to outlast him. “If anyone has any ideas on how to change the name of a political movement,” Frost says, “let me know.”

#3484. Final Fantasy 7 Remake Director Confirms He Doesn’t Let Fans’ Reactions Shape His Games

The final chapter in the Final Fantasy 7 remake trilogy, Final Fantasy 7: Revelation, is just a few months away. Speculation is growing about how Square Enix and the development team will bring the game to a close, with fans sharing their own opinions and theories on what to expect when it debuts this April.

One thing remains clear, however: Naoki Hamaguchi, the game director behind the series' reimagining, has always known the direction of the trilogy — and fan feedback does not factor into it.

The changes surrounding Remake and Rebirth — such as the introduction of the Whispers and Zack Fair’s role — have always been a hot topic for fans to debate. The Whispers, for example, were not involved at all in the original game, so their appearance fundamentally changed how fans perceived the events of Remake and Rebirth, and we can assume Revelation.

While some fans welcome the new themes, characters, and features, others worry that Final Fantasy 7’s new direction could reimagine the original so extensively that its story becomes unrecognizable.

However, in a social media post on X, Hamaguchi set the record straight about the direction the developers are taking with Final Fantasy 7.

“We believe it’s our responsibility as creators to decide the major direction of the story, rather than having it shaped by fan reactions. Together with a new generation of developers, we’re reimagining FINAL FANTASY VII for today.”

Furthermore, in an interview with Xbox Dynasty, Hamaguchi explained that the original creators of Final Fantasy 7 ultimately have the final say on any changes to the story, with younger developers on the team reimagining “familiar content from the original for modern players.”

As fans, we naturally have opinions about the things we love — that’s what makes us fans. Still, it’s reassuring to hear Hamaguchi make clear that the development team isn’t swayed by shifting fan opinions. Focus groups and fan screenings can help creators feel confident that people will enjoy their work, but that approach can also feel clinical, even dishonest. Creatives want their work to succeed both financially and critically, but catering only to what fans want risks costing them their creative vision.

At least, that doesn’t seem to be a risk with Revelation. Whether it pays off for Square Enix and the team remains to be seen when Final Fantasy 7: Revelation releases on April 8, 2027.

#3483. This 75-inch Hisense Mini-LED TV Is Nearly Half Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3482. Bill Pullman Starred In This '90s Neo-Noir Drama That Tried Suing The Oscars

Before we discuss John Dahl's "The Last Seduction" starring Linda Fiorentino and Bill Pullman, let's set the table. In the indispensable documentary "A Personal Journey With Martin Scorsese Through American Movies," the legendary director discusses the concept of artistic smuggling. The idea is that clever filmmakers can slip subversive themes past unsophisticated producers who are more focused on making a tidy profit than crafting a movie that means and says something.

Back in the B-movie heyday of the 1950s, this practice was common, particularly in genre pictures. Film noir offered a particularly fertile ground for such felonious messing around. Tales of compromised characters doing the wrong thing to get over or simply survive resonated in the wake of the Great Depression and World War II. People knew hard times and found cruel catharsis in watching folks trying, and typically failing, to game the system.

Noir never went away. It mutated with the ever-troubled times, as any fraught moment in American history could serve as the backdrop for a sexy, politically charged thriller. Then third-wave feminism hit in the 1990s, and femmes fatales became protagonists. And we were rooting for them.

It's hard to top the great Sharon Stone as Catherine Tramell in Paul Verhoeven's "Basic Instinct," but I think the best third-wave femme fatale is Fiorentino's Bridget Gregory in "The Last Seduction." From the minute her dirtbag husband, Clay (Pullman), slaps her for insulting him, she begins spinning a complex web that will lead to his undoing. Fiorentino is magnificent every step of the way, and she would've waltzed into a Best Actress Oscar had the film been treated with the respect it deserved. Alas, despite a lawsuit to get her into contention, the Academy refused to budge. And this is a case where smuggling might've hurt a film noir.

In a 2015 interview with Creative Screenwriting, "The Last Seduction" screenwriter Steve Barancik explained the film's creatives pitched the movie to ITC Entertainment as standard-issue Skinemax sleaze. John Dahl, of course, aspired to make a high-quality neo-noir, and once the film's actors read Barancik's script, they knew the project had a chance to be something special. That's how the movie attracted respected names like Linda Fiorentino (who demanded Dahl cast her), Bill Pullman, Peter Berg, Bill Nunn, Dean Norris, and the dearly missed J.T. Walsh.

When an ITC executive panicked early on, the filmmakers got a tongue-lashing. "He shut down production and called the principals of the movie on the carpet, and they all had to pledge that they had no artistic pretensions," Barancik recalled. After the film was completed, ITC sold it off to HBO before it could get theatrical distribution. Unfortunately, if a movie doesn't get an Oscar qualifying run in theaters, it's ineligible for consideration. Again, the distributor October Films brought a suit against the Academy on Fiorentino's behalf, but the organization's rules were clear: no qualifying run, no nomination.

Fiorentino did earn Best Actress prizes from the Independent Spirit Awards and the New York Film Critics Circle, but she likely would've won the Best Actress Oscar if she'd been allowed to compete. (Instead, the prize went to a deserving Jessica Lange for making a meal out of her role in Tony Richardson's film "Blue Sky.") I don't blame Dahl and company for their smuggling gambit, but ticking off ITC was a costly mistake.

Sing Sing was one of my favorite movies of 2024 and one of the best movies of that year. Colman Domingo shines. He once again proves that he’s one of the best actors of his generation. Domingo’s brilliant scene partners, many not professionally trained actors, magnify his performance.

Using former Sing Sing Prison inmates, and some of those the story was based on, was a revolutionary idea. When I saw Union County, I became more convinced that films should enlist locals or real-life inspirations so those stories appear as characters in more films.

Will Poulter plays Cody, a man in a court-ordered recovery program in Union County. He’s doing fairly well in it until he reunites with his foster brother Jack (Noah Centineo). The film depicts both of their struggles to stay sober, while also highlighting these recovery programs and the people who use them. I first saw Union County at the Davis Theater in Chicago at a special screening with Poulter in attendance.

He explained his experiences with making the movie and having real people from Union County in it. You feel that community throughout. It, in a way, makes Union County feel more grounded in reality than other films with similar topics.

Addiction and recovery are popular subjects in art. Union County may be among the best films about addiction because it feels intimate and quiet while honestly and organically tackling addiction and recovery. Director Adam Meeks puts respect and care into the film’s authenticity and highlights the community without judgment.

I love hearing filmmakers, actors, and creatives speak about their work. You get a better understanding of the process and intentions behind things. You also get a firsthand look at the passion for the project. Therefore, I enjoyed hearing Poulter speak about the importance Meeks and he put into their work with the community. Someone in the audience at the Davis Theater showing knew a person who appeared in the film. She therefore further highlighted how the community bonded even more while making Union County.

Many actors carry the prejudgment that they don’t like working or associating with those outside the acting and filmmaking world. Therefore, it is refreshing to see and hear about those who care about working with all scene partners, whether they’re an extra or an Oscar-winning actor, with the same courtesy, respect, and compassion.

Union County digs into the many aspects of addiction, including mental health. It’s another very honest movie about the mental struggles of addiction. Effectively showcasing things like the mental health struggles of addiction likely comes from consulting those with addiction while creating this film.

Besides Poulter and Centineo’s brilliant performances, Union County gets a lot of its power and authenticity from the people in the community playing extras or small roles. They don’t feel like people playing a part but those putting their real life on the screen in one way or another. It’s these types of lived experiences that make movies such as Sing Sing and Union County unique but also profound.

Many movies are all about escapism, while others remind you of the tragedy and hope of everyday life. The latter films often stay with you longer. It’s more transformative when those who understand the experience of the characters personally participate in the making of movies.

My wife, Janice. Fearless, smart, optimistic, hilarious, loving…adored by all.

Self-doubt. Wait, now I’m not sure of the answer. Was that okay? Can we come back to that one?

From my dressing room to backstage—standing alone in the dark, a deep breath, and then feeling it’s time and walking out into the light.

That my father died when I was 15 and never got to see my family, my career, and the man I think I am.

In the hospital waiting room, when my girls were born, and the doctor said everyone was fine.

I’d stop worrying about everyone all the time.

That they’d finally understand why I worry about everyone all the time

We raised two fantastic daughters who became good, hard-working, honest people and great spouses and mothers in the middle of this business.

#3479. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3478. 36 Years Later, Home Alone's Best Line Is Still The Funniest Christmas Movie Quote Ever

"Home Alone," as directed by Chris Columbus (who later kicked off the "Harry Potter" movie franchise), is an undisputed Christmas comedy classic. But while there are definitely yuletide themes of appreciating your family, the film also has a mean streak several miles wide.

If you've somehow never seen it, "Home Alone" follows eight-year-old Kevin McCallister (Macaulay Culkin) after his large family accidentally leaves him at home in Chicago while running late for a Christmas vacation flight to Paris. Kevin, whose family either ignores or bullies him, at first relishes being alone before coming to miss his relatives. Meanwhile, two burglars, the "Wet Bandits" Harry (Joe Pesci) and Marv (Daniel Stern), plan to rob the McCallister house. Thus, in the third act, Kevin fills his home with comical but extremely painful booby traps. (The Wet Bandits' physical misfortune is the closest filmmaking has come to recreating "Looney Tunes" slapstick in purely live-action.)

"Home Alone" was the second highest grossing film of 1990 behind "Ghost," but it received only decent reviews overall. To this day, the movie has a positive but unimpressive rating of 66% positive on Rotten Tomatoes and a similar 63% on Metacritic. Roger Ebert gave the film 2.5/4 stars in his contemporary review, praising Culkin's charm but criticizing the Wet Bandits' subplot.

"[Because] all plausibility is gone, we sit back, detached, to watch stunt men and special effects guys take over a movie that promised to be the kind of story audiences could identify with," Ebert wrote. Yet, for most others, that implausibility is what makes "Home Alone" so funny.

As part of Kevin's new freedom, he watches grown-up movies like the fictional black and white gangster film "Angels with Filthy Souls." The movie shows one scene where a gangster named Johnny (Ralph Foody) refuses to pay another criminal, Snakes (Michael Guido), and then shoots Snakes with a Tommy gun.

"I'm gonna give you to the count of 10 to get your ugly, yella, no-good keister off my property, before I pump your guts full of lead!" Johnny declares, skipping straight from two to 10. "Keep the change, ya filthy animal," Johnny declares as Kevin covers his eyes and shuts off the movie.

Kevin later plays a cruel trick on an unsuspecting pizza boy (D. Danny Warhol) by carefully pausing and fast forwarding/rewinding the movie at the right moments from inside the house. ("What money?" Johnny asks Snakes. "Well, you have to pay for your pizza, sir," the delivery boy explains.) Later, when Marv comes snooping around the house, Kevin lets the scene play out in full to make him think he wandered into a gang deal that turned deadly. This time, Kevin uses firecrackers to simulate the sound of gunfire and also mouths Johnny's "Keep the change, ya filthy animal."

"Home Alone 2" repeated the gag with a sequel, "Angels with Even Filthier Souls," where Johnny guns down his girlfriend (Clare Hoak) for supposedly sleeping around behind his back. There, it's arguably even funnier because it's a Plaza Hotel concierge (the much-missed Tim Curry) reacting to the prank and ultimately concluding, "There's an insane guest with a gun!" Some would argue that "Home Alone 2" is even better than its predecessor, and "Angels with Even Filthier Souls" is definitely a case where going bigger proved better.

#3477. Johnny Depp Tops the Box Office Again With Ebenezer's Opening Weekend

Ebenezer opened the festive season in theaters this weekend

With December fast approaching, the holiday cheer is quickly creeping up on moviegoers around the world. The festive season kicked off with the premiere of Ebenezer in theaters on Nov. 13. The story of Ebenezer Scrooge was originally told in Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol, published in late 1843. Nearly two centuries later, the morals that are taught in A Christmas Carol remain relevant, and it is hard not to be touched by Scrooge's transformation from a Grinch-like miser into a generous man.

This story has been retold and adapted dozens of times. The latest adaptation of A Christmas Carol is director Ti West's Ebenezer starring Johnny Depp as Scrooge, Rupert Grint as Bob Cratchit, and Ian McKellen as Jacob Marley. The retelling of this classic tale received a neutral rating from critics, only reaching 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. However, audiences disagreed, giving it a 90% rating. It was able to snag moviegoers' attention on its opening weekend, earning $19 million in its opening weekend in the US and a further $23 million internationally.

Johnny Depp, the main focus of this movie, remained out of the spotlight for years due to a lengthy legal battle with his ex-wife Amber Heard involving domestic abuse allegations. Many reviewers have tied the movie's rating to the actor, which has tipped the scales both ways.

Peter Travers from The Travers Take remarks: "Depp is still the kind of talent who can make you feel a character’s pain. Both he and Ebenezer are looking for absolution. Dickens took care of Ebenezer. Depp’s fate is up to the audience. I’m rooting for him." Amy Nicholson from the LA Times believes that "the actor’s need to be loved — to claw himself out of what he fears is an early career grave, an image we see him physically do — hijacks the movie. The traditional beats don’t land."

According to Variety, half of those that attended the premiere watched Ebenezer to see Johnny Depp, as it was his first major role in eight years. His next appearance will be in Day Drinker, scheduled for March 26, 2027. He is also currently in talks with Disney to return as Jack Sparrow in the next Pirates of the Caribbean.

#3476. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3475. Star Trek's Leonard Nimoy Would Only Appear As Spock In Public Under One Condition

For many actors, playing an iconic role in a beloved series can be a bit of a mixed blessing. On the one hand, you've got the success, fame, and the knowledge that your performance has become part of the cultural zeitgeist and touched the lives of millions of fans across the world. On the other, though, there's the risk of being typecast or ignored for roles that could show your range, overzealous fans who confuse your personal thoughts and feelings with those of your character, and the occasional circus that wants to put you on display like a sideshow act. Those extremes are naturally going to be exacerbated when you're playing one of the most iconic characters in the history of television.

Such was the case for Leonard Nimoy, who found worldwide fame playing Mr. Spock on the original "Star Trek," and developed a somewhat complicated relationship with his overly logical alter-ego, going as far as titling his first autobiography "I Am Not Spock," before calling his second "I Am Spock" 20 years later. For him, though, it seems that the worst part wasn't the typecasting or the fans, but those famous pointy ears. As he revealed in an interview with the Philadelphia Inquirer (via MeTV) during the original run of "Star Trek," he was willing to appear as Spock in public, but only if he didn't have to wear his character's signature makeup.

While his time in the makeup chair certainly wasn't as arduous as later "Trek" actors like Michael Dorn, whose Worf costuming took a two and a half hours during the early seasons of "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Nimoy was not a fan of the pointed, alien ears that became a trademark of his character. He even struck a deal with "Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry to give Spock an in-universe ear surgery if Nimoy didn't get used to them by the end of the show's first 13 episodes. Even the network executives initially thought they were a bad idea, less for Nimoy's discomfort and more because of the fear that audiences would see Spock as a demonic figure — a worry they got over really quickly once they saw how popular the first officer of the "Enterprise" was with fans.

Nimoy, of course, eventually got used to wearing the ears on set, presumably due at least in part to an increase in salary after Spock was almost cut from the show's second season. Off the set, though, he flatly refused to wear them in other appearances, as he told the Inquirer in 1968:

"Spock and his makeup are okay within a dramatic environment, but not outside. [...] I turned down $50,000 last year, because I won't make personal appearances in makeup, except for my hair which I don't mind."

Keep in mind that this is $50,000 in 1967. While that might be a worthless sum in the post-scarcity utopian future of "Star Trek," it's the equivalent of over $512,000 in today's money. Sure, it's important to draw a line between actor and character, but for half a million bucks, you probably wouldn't have a hard time finding someone willing to have their ears pointed permanently.

Nimoy, however, apparently valued the roundness of his lobes more than the money, a dilemma that would've torn Ferengi society apart if it had happened within the "Star Trek" universe. If only he'd come up with the ear-hiding headband look that he rocked in "Star Trek IV" a few decades earlier (seen in the screenshot above), Nimoy could've had it all.
