#3474. The 13 Best International Fantasy TV Shows, Ranked

Fantasy is a very old genre of fiction, one that is well over two centuries old at this point. It has lasted so long because there is just something so captivating about worlds full of magic and monsters, or that feature aspects that are so far beyond our current existence. It's kind of hard not to get wrapped up in these worlds, especially with the rise of fantasy television, which has become more popular than ever since the 2010s started.

While there are a lot of English-language fantasy shows out there that deserve widespread success, they aren't all that can be found in the world of fantasy. Indeed, many countries around the world have tried their hand at fantasy, often to incredible results. Whether it's romantasy, supernatural drama, or fantasy horror, there's something out there for everybody, regardless of language. These are the best international fantasy TV shows of all time.

This Chinese series is honestly one of the most entertaining watches in the animated genre. Scissor Seven centers on an amnesiac hairdresser named Seven (Xiaofeng He), who moonlights as a spectacularly incompetent assassin while wielding telekinetically controlled scissors.

Scissor Seven is quite the silly indulgence, yet it’s pretty surprising how nonsense tends to become addictive drama within the show. Initially, the series uses its earlier episodes to deliver tons of parody martial-arts clichés, but as the show goes on, it keeps adding emotional consequence without losing its strange comedy. With its unique trajectory, Scissor Seven makes for some pretty memorable TV. Its unusual balance creates an animated experience that feels genuinely heartfelt, exciting, and consistently surprising, making it an easy pick for this list due to the show’s fine demonstration of contemporary Chinese animation. —Jiminna Shillingford

Mortel, which translates to "Mortal," is about two high schoolers named Sofiane (Carl Malapa) and Victor (Némo Schiffman), who are thrust into a rough situation when Sofiane's brother is murdered. Desperate for answers, Sofiane and Victor make a pact with an ancient voodoo god, giving them supernatural powers to aid them in their quest for justice. Accompanying them is voodoo practitioner Luisa (Manon Bresch), who is there to ensure the voodoo god doesn't trick the two into falling for his trap.

Mortel wasn't super popular, and it's pretty far from amazing, but it's enjoyable nonetheless. It feels like a blend of superhero dramas and fantasy shows, with a really interesting dynamic between Sofiane and Victor. The two have different sets of powers, but they don't function unless they're near each other, which opens up a lot of doors for plot twists and obstacles. Mortel is a great show for those who like supernatural dramas and murder mysteries.

Ragnarok takes its title from Norse mythology — the term "Ragnarok" refers to armageddon, when the gods will die, the sun will go out, and the world will come to a violent, destructive end. The series, naturally, is set in a remote town in Norway, which has fallen under the shadow of the tyrannical Jutul family. The Jutuls are business owners and oversee a series of factories that are polluting the picturesque Norwegian village. Little do the townsfolk know, however, that the Jutuls are actually supernatural beings called jötnar.

With the Jutuls oppressing the townsfolk, the fate of the village, and possibly of the world, falls into the hands of Magne (David Stakston), who learns that he is the reincarnation of the Norse god of thunder, Thor. Ragnarok isn't amazing, but it's very entertaining, and it was lucky enough to get three seasons, which is more than most shows get. It wasn't a huge hit domestically, but it has received a higher level of praise internationally, particularly in English-speaking countries.

If I Hadn't Met You hails from Spain, but is actually in Catalan rather than Spanish. The harrowing drama series follows Eduard (Pablo Derqui), a heartbroken man who has lost his entire family in a gruesome car accident. Devastated and adrift in life, Eduard seeks the help of Liz Everest (Mercedes Sampietro), who teaches Eduard to unlock the supernatural power contained within him, which allows him to travel to alternate universes.

This leads Eduard on a quest to find an alternate universe in which his family has survived, so that he can seek some respite from his suffering. The ten-part series only received one season, but honestly, that's all it really needed. Reviews are generally pretty positive, with viewers commending the series for its emotion and heartfelt storyline. The acting performances are also really incredible, with Pablo Derqui perfectly capturing Eduard's sense of profound sorrow and loss.

Trese is a fascinating international animated series that’s the perfect mesh of horror, mystery, and cultural storytelling. Based on the Filipino comic series by Budjette Tan and Kajo Baldisimo, the series centers around an investigator known as Alexandra Trese (Shay Mitchell) who operates at the boundary between the supernatural communities hidden within the Philippine capital and ordinary criminal cases.

Trese is an easy pick for this list because it brings supernatural creatures and the ancient legends of Philippine folklore into a rather dark and intriguing modern setting. The show's standout appeal is its sense that the setting, Manila itself, is part of the mythology. With just a limited, six-episode structure, Trese delivers the perfect supernatural show, one that is worthwhile for viewers who want adult fantasy animation that goes beyond the generic European tropes featuring demons, vampires, and fairy tales. —Jiminna Shillingford

LastMan is a truly underrated international joy that offers a distinctive combination of intense action, French animation, and supernatural mystery. Set in the corrupt city of Paxtown, the adventure fantasy follows the boxer Richard Aldana (Martial Le Minoux), who becomes responsible for protecting young Siri (Maëlys Ricordeau) from violent supernatural forces.

With its mature storytelling and energetic fight sequences, LastMan makes for a great example of international animation intended for older viewers. It’s a brilliant series that definitely deserves its flowers and far more attention, especially because French animation rarely gets associated internationally with hard-edged adult action TV, yet LastMan delivers exactly that while consistently maintaining its charming European art style. LastMan is a genuine gem that may not enjoy the popularity it truly deserves but is an excellent example of one of the best animated series ever made. —Jiminna Shillingford

Love Between Fairy and Devil is a show that cuts right to the chase with its title. It's pretty easy to infer what the plot is about, but just in case you need clarification, the unforgettable romance-fantasy series follows Dongfang Qingcang (Dylan Wang), the Demon King known as the Moon Supreme. During a war in which the Demon King assaulted the heavens, he was sealed away, only to be released by the goddess of war. Millennia later, the war goddess is reborn in the form of Xiao Lunhua (Yu Shuxin), also known as Orchid.

This is a show for all those romantasy fans out there. Featuring a touching love story of forbidden romance between immortal beings on opposite sides of the good and evil dynamic, Love Between Fairy and Devil garnered very positive reviews from international audiences, particularly in East and Southeast Asia. The first and only season consists of a whopping 36 episodes, none of which are boring or bad. Romantasay isn't a genre for everyone, and it's understandable if that's the case, but for those who do like the subgenre, this show is a must-see.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

One Piece is one of the longest-running anime series ever, which has been going strong for 26 years. The series is primarily pirate-themed, with the plot hinging on a coveted pirate map that supposedly leads to untold treasures. Unfortunately, one piece of the map is missing, prompting a search across the Seven Seas for it, hence the title. The main character is an aspiring young pirate named Monkey D. Luffy, who has eaten a magical Devil Fruit, which allows him to stretch and rubberize his body at will.

The series is definitely mature, but also humorous and light-hearted. There are loads of action and thrills at sea, all accentuated by magic and mystery. One Piece has become such a staple of television that it even inspired a live-action remake on Netflix in 2023. However, the original series still reigns supreme — aside from being the best pirate show of all time, it's easily one of the greatest fantasy shows of all time, too.

Shahmaran is a Turkish series named after the mythical creature of the same name. The fantastical Şahmaran is purported to be half-woman, half-snake, and has roots in Turkish and Indo-Iranian folklore. The main character is Şahsu (Serenay Sarıkaya), a psychology professor from the Crossroads of the World — Istanbul. Şahsu moves to the smaller city of Adana for work, and while there, encounters a cult that worships Şahmaran, who are patiently awaiting the fulfillment of some sort of prophecy. Things get stranger when Şahsu meets a strange man named Maran (Burak Deniz).

Spanning two seasons, Shahmaran was commended for the performances of its main cast, as well as the family dynamics that occur both inside and outside of the cult. It was also praised for its mysterious premise, especially with the sense of intrigue that surrounds the cult. Domestically popular, yet internationally unheard of, Shahmaran is one of the most underrated Netflix original series that deserves to be seen by any fantasy fan.

Alchemy of Souls consists of two seasons and 30 episodes, with each season following its own distinct storylines, which are mostly separate but still connected to each other. The series follows mages in the fictional country of Daeho, who begin a dangerous quest to learn a forbidden spell that will allow them to switch bodies. In the process, a renowned warrior becomes trapped in a weakened body, yet still falls in love with a young nobleman.

This is another show that is largely a romantasy, which isn't everyone's personal cup of tea, so it's understandable if you're averse to checking this one out. However, for people who love a romantic subplot to go with their magic, Alchemy of Souls is about as good as it gets, bearing all the hallmarks of a classic K-drama with a twist of fantasy, all set in a vaguely Medieval world.

Same and I have shared it with everyone I know. Definitely deserved at least number 2.

#3473. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3472. What Is The Covey In The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping?

Within the world of the two "Hunger Games" prequels — "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping" — there's a group called the Covey, and two of their young women are major influences on the narratives. So, who are the Covey, exactly?

So, "covey" is a real word. According to Merriam-Webster, it refers to "a mature bird or pair of birds with a brood of young" (or "a small flock"). This is perfect, because the two major Covey characters in this franchise — Lucy Gray Baird, played by Rachel Zegler, and Lenore Dove Baird, played by Whitney Peak, in the film versions of "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping," respectively — are often referred to by the men who love and despise them as birds of some sort. Again, though: what is the Covey?

In the "Sunrise on the Reaping" novel by Suzanne Collins, Lenore Dove's boyfriend and our protagonist Haymitch (played by Joseph Zada in the movie adaptation) informs the reader that, when Lenore Dove occasionally sings for him in their private refuge of a nearby meadow, it's particularly special because "she never does it in public." He adds, "None of the Covey do. Her uncles are really more musicians than singers, so they just play tunes and leave the singing to the audience if they're so inclined."

Those uncles — Clerk Carmine and Tam Amber, the former of whom appears in the film version and is played by Jeffrey Hallman — took Lenore Dove in, though Haymitch notes that her father was always "something of a mystery." (Note that shared last name of "Baird," though.) So, are the musically inclined folks in the Covey from District 12? That's complicated. (Also, they did sing before the events of "Sunrise on the Reaping.")

So, what's the deal with the Covey's origin? As Haymitch notes in "Sunrise on the Reaping," they have a dark backstory. "Her people were great travelers once, going from district to district to perform their music," he recalls. "Tam Amber remembers it, as he was about my age when the war ended and the Peacekeepers rounded up the Covey, killing all the adults and confining the kids to our district."

This is exactly what Lucy Gray Baird tells a young Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth in the film adaptation), the future president of the dystopian region of Panem, and a Capitol reporter during "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" as she prepares to fight as the District 12 tribute in the 10th Hunger Games. As she puts it in the book version of the story, "'It's Lucy Gray and I'm not really from [12]. My people are Covey. Musicians by trade. We just took a wrong turn one day and were obliged to stay.'"

When asked which district the Covey does come from, Lucy Gray provides an explanation: "'No district in particular. We move from place to place as the fancy takes us.' Lucy Gray caught herself. 'Well, we used to anyway. Before the Peacekeepers rounded us up a few years back.'" When the reporter tries to clarify that this makes her a District 12 denizen, she loses interest in the conversation. Also, remember how I mentioned singing? Lenore Dove's generation of the Covey might not love singing in public, but Lucy Gray famously does in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" ... and it helps her charm audiences and even win the Hunger Games at the time.

District 12 is the only district we've seen pretty comprehensively in the "Hunger Games" franchise as of this writing (it's possible that Suzanne Collins could write a prequel set in a different district), and the rules are a little looser there across all the books. Capitol Peacekeepers tend to allow sales of illicit materials like the white liquor to which Haymitch ultimately becomes addicted, and they also allow concerts from the Covey, which we see prominently featured in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." In the book version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch shares that these privileges have continued years after Lucy Gray's live performances:

"[The Covey] worked out a deal with the mayor, whose house boasts the only real piano in District 12. Lenore Dove can practice on it if she plays during an occasional dinner or gathering. Her in a faded green dress, an ivory ribbon tying back her hair, lips tinted orange. When her family performs around District 12 for money, she makes do with the instrument she is playing now, which she calls her tune box."

Essentially, the Covey is a musical group who play instruments and sing — well, the latter depends on the timeframe — and were traveling artists before the districts of Panem fully formed. Between their preference for brightly colored clothes, their musical talents, and their yearning for freedom, the Covey stand out in Panem ... and two of its number, Lucy Gray and Lenore Dove, are extraordinarily important to the story.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on November 20, 2026.

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3470. D&D’s World of Warcraft Book Fixes the RPG’s Biggest Endgame Issue

WoW understands what big, scary monsters need in D&D

WoW understands what big, scary monsters need in D&D

It’s no secret that, in Dungeons & Dragons, the job of a Dungeon Master gets increasingly harder as the player characters rise in level. Building challenging encounters for a high-level party can be daunting. In the past, I wrote about how high challenge rating (CR) monsters often feel inadequate to perform the task of “end-game bosses,” unless a DM puts measures in place (such as the use of minions) that, however, can have a negative impact on the game.

Let’s imagine that the big bad of a D&D campaign is a powerful devil, such as a Pit Fiend. The monster has a CR of 20, but that doesn’t mean it will prove a good challenge for a level-20 party — quite the opposite: the poor devil doesn’t stand a chance. A good DM can make the encounter harder by adding more creatures to act as backup, but that means having to run a dozen monsters instead of one, which can slow down combat significantly. Also, grinding through endless cannon fodder may not be fun for players who have waited months (or years) to kick the villain’s butt.

Complex problems like these require creative solutions. That’s where the latest D&D book, World of Warcraft, comes in. The new book presents several high-CR monsters that can provide a solid challenge on their own for high-level parties. The solution is deceptively simple: Just hit them all at once.

The discrepancy between player characters and monsters in D&D’s 5th edition (and in its 5.5e expansion) can be summed up in three main issues: numbers, scaling, and resources.

By their most common cultural understanding, monsters are solitary creatures. It’s part of the mystique of the “monster” concept: an aberrant entity that doesn’t fit within the laws of society or nature. Of course, D&D players are all familiar with goblin armies or swarms of carrion crawlers (yuck!), but these monsters are usually low-level: strength in numbers and all that. Once you move up the ladder, monsters often keep to themselves.

D&D, however, is not a solo game. Adventuring parties are usually composed of a minimum of four characters, and that number can go up, depending on how deranged the DM is (personally, anything more than five would quickly lead me to a nervous breakdown). For a fight between adventurers and a monster to be “fair,” the latter should be at least four times as powerful as a single player character. But that’s never the case.

This very French werewolf is no longer one of the scariest monsters in Ravenloft

The problem with the challenge rating system (and the encounter-building guidelines provided in the Dungeon Master’s Guide) is that player characters do not scale up in power in a linear way, but monsters do. A CR 6 monster will usually be twice as “strong” as a CR 3 one, whereas a level 6 character is many times more powerful than a level 3 one. This is because characters acquire increasingly complex abilities, spells, and magic items. Their progress is not linear, and almost exponential.

Finally, the whole 5th edition of D&D is designed not to be fair to monsters because of its grindy nature. Character classes are built on resource management. A D&D party is expected to have two or three combat encounters in each adventuring day, before needing a long rest to refresh their resources. This means that, if the only encounter a level 5 party faces in a day is a CR 5 or 6 monster, the poor critter will quickly get annihilated. Instead, the DM is supposed to feed the party a couple of lower-level encounters beforehand. But what if that doesn’t fit the story, or the party is just good at avoiding unnecessary combat?

The World of Warcraft book has 15 monsters of CR 20 or higher, only six fewer than the entire Monster Manual. In the MMORPG, there are many powerful “raid bosses” that require a great deal of teamwork to defeat, and the book succeeds in translating that mechanic to D&D. High-level monsters in World of Warcraft are designed to face multiple players, which immediately fixes the first issue with D&D monsters: numbers.

World of Warcraft monsters are all designed with area attacks or other crowd-control options. This means they can hit multiple player characters at once, or separate and isolate party members effectively, thus reducing the need to add extra bodies to a fight just to keep some players busy.

You can look at any high-level monster in the World of Warcraft book, and it will invariably have at least one AoE (area of effect) attack. But two comparisons are particularly meaningful, because they involve WoW monsters that have almost exact duplicates in the Monster Manual.

The Red Dragonflight Dragon is, unsurprisingly, World of Warcraft’s version of an Ancient Red Dragon. While the Dragonflight has a slightly lower CR of 21 compared to the Ancient’s 24 (and, accordingly, fewer hit points), the WoW version does a much better job at keeping a whole party occupied.

Both dragons have a breath attack and a one-use-per-day AoE spell (Fireball for the Ancient and Flame Strike for the Dragonflight). Both can cast Command at level 2 at will. The Ancient also has a level 3 Scorching Ray available at will, but it substitutes one of its Rend attacks. The Dragonflight, instead, has a legendary action called Bellowing Roar, which hits every creature in a 30-foot cube, dealing thunder damage and pushing the targets away. It can only be used once per turn, but it truly makes the difference, giving the dragon a free AoE attack that also moves its enemies around, as a great alternative to the breath attack (which recharges on a 5-6 for both dragons).

The book is experimenting with complex boss fights and transformative subclasses

The other example is World of Warcraft’s Pit Lord, a demon that is almost an exact copy of the Pit Fiend from the Monster Manual. They have the same CR of 20 and most of the same traits and abilities, including the excellent Fear Aura. However, the Pit Lord gets another AoE option in the form of the Rain of Felfire action, which hits every creature in a 30-foot radius with both fire and psychic damage. It also gets Trampling Charge as a bonus action, which lets the Pit Lord move up to its speed, hitting every creature in its path for bludgeoning damage and a chance to knock them prone.

The Pit Fiend, on the other hand, only gets a Hellfire Spellcasting action, which lets it cast Fireball twice, or one Fireball plus a Hold Monster or Wall of Fire. It’s very powerful, but it recharges on a roll of 4-6, so on average it only works once every two turns. It’s also weak against characters who have resistance to fire damage (which can be expected if the party is prepared to face a devil).

Overall, it’s clear how these World of Warcraft monsters are built with Area of Effect and crowd control effects in mind, which makes them better endgame bosses for a party of high-level characters. This exposes some big design flaws in D&D 5th edition, at least when it comes to monsters. Nowhere is this clearer than when you look at some of the most powerful monsters that appeared in the core D&D books.

The second-highest CR monster in the Monster Manual is the CR 25 Colossus (beaten only by the Tarrasque). The Colossus has exactly one area attack: its Divine Beam action, which is massive, but it recharges on a 5-6 and replaces its other actions. This looks particularly ridiculous because this is a gargantuan size construct that towers over buildings, and yet its Stomp attack only hits one creature.

If we look at Monsters of the Multiverse instead (a book that introduced many of the 5.5e updates early), we can find one of the most iconic endgame monsters in D&D: Demogorgon, Prince of Demons, the Sibilant Beast, and a massive wimp. Despite its CR of 26, Demogorgon is not the deadly challenge that player characters of that level would expect. It has only two attacks, which can be a combination of Tentacle and Gaze. The latter is powerful and can mess up a party with confusion, charm, and stun effects, but it still has a single target. Demogorgon’s only AoE attack is its 3-per-day use of the spell Fear – which replaces its other attacks.

As a side note, Demogorgon also has less HP than Lich King Arthas.

This doesn’t mean that you should try to jam WoW characters and creatures into all your high-level D&D campaigns. But there are important lessons that can be learned from the World of Warcraft book.

High-level monsters should have multiple AoE attacks and crowd control effects. This balances the numbers game, which is usually in favor of the adventurers, without needing to add mobs to the encounter (and thus making the DM’s job easier!). If the party attacks a monster four or five times in a combat round, then it’s only fair for the monster to hit multiple party members in the same round.

It’s not hard to design an AoE attack for your homebrewed monsters, or add one to the creatures presented in the Monster Manual. Reskinning and customizing monsters may look complicated, but it’s a great skill for a DM to have. Adding or subtracting traits and actions or tinkering with a monster’s damage, attacks, and HP can turn a boring encounter into a challenging one on the fly.

If you’re looking for guidance on how to improve combat encounters, I suggest checking out Keith Ammann’s books, Mike Shea’s Lazy Dungeon Master series, or checking the Sly Flourish website for free resources.

#3469. All Upcoming Owen Wilson Movies & TV Shows, Including Focker-In-Law

Owen Wilson is one of the most popular actors and comedians of the last 25 years. He’s appeared in countless classics, from the Meet the Parents franchise to Disney’s iconic Cars films. Wilson always tends to incorporate his classic comedic charm into every role, all while making each character truly stand out.

Wilson is showing no signs of slowing down, either. The actor is currently working on a number of projects, some of which are follow-ups to his classic films (such as the upcoming Focker-in-Law, which releases in theaters this holiday season).

Interestingly, Owen Wilson has branched out in recent years, appearing in more serious roles as well as comedies. That’s different from Wilson’s early career, which saw him appear mostly as the “funny man,” (with a few exceptions) in projects like Wedding Crashers and Starksy and Hutch.

Moving forward, Wilson continues that streak, with some projects you’d expect from the actor, while also having some bolder moves lined up, too. The last time the actor appeared on the big screen was in Avengers: Endgame Encore (out now on Disney+), in which he showed up in one of the four additional post credits scenes added to the film.

As of now, it’s not clear if Wilson will appear in the cast of Avengers: Doomsday, or if the scene from Encore was filmed specifically for the film’s rerelease. Regardless, the actor has a number of exciting movies and shows coming up for his fans to look forward to.

Owen Wilson’s longest running role in his career is, perhaps surprisingly, not Lightning McQueen from the Cars franchise. Instead, that title belongs to Kevin Rawley, the character that Wilson plays in Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro’s family comedy franchise that began with Meet the Parents.

Wilson is set to appear in Focker-in-Law, which comes out in theaters this holiday season. Wilson once again plays Rawley, an unusual figure who is a favorite of Jack Byrnes (De Niro) and was once engaged to Greg Focker’s wife, Pam. All of these are back in the new movie, and they’re joined by two new characters — Skyler Gisondo’s Henry Focker and Ariana Grande’s Olivia Jones.

As stated, there is no official confirmation on whether or not Owen Wilson will appear in Avengers: Doomsday, the highly anticipated Marvel Studios film which premieres next month. However, his presence in one of the the post-credits scenes of Avengers: Endgame Encore provides strong evidence that Wilson might be making another MCU appearance.

The post-credits scene was directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, who are helming Doomsday, which serves as further evidence of Wilson’s potential appearance next month. Not only that, but another TVA member is in Doomsday, too — Tom Hiddelston’s Loki. And, like Owen Wilson, Hiddelston appears in one of the added post-credits scenes in Endgame: Encore, which shows him arriving at Steve Rogers' house in the 1950s.

Wilson will reprise his role as Lightning McQueen next year in Cars: Lightning Racers, which is currently in post-production. Lightning Racers is a different kind of Cars project, however, and will release on Disney+ next year. The new series will be primarily geared towards young school-aged children, and has a unique animation style to boot, too.

The visual style of Lightning Racers is similar to that of the Cars films, so classic characters like Lightning McQueen and Mater will still be recognizable. Both are returning for the new series, as are other characters like Pipes, Miles, and Ms. Blinker.

Cars: Lightning Racers will take an episodic approach, with each episode focusing on a new adventure in the lives of Lightning McQueen and co. Along with McQueen and the returning characters, there are reportedly a number of new heroes created for the new show that will make their Cars franchise debut next year.

This show marks the sixteenth different project that Owen Wilson voices Lightning McQueen in. The actor helped to launch the franchise in 2006 with the first Cars film, and has since gone on to play the iconic character in a number of follow-up movies and shows. While there hasn’t been a Cars film since 2017’s Cars 3, in which Lightning McQueen serves as the mentor to Cruz Ramirez, Wilson has also appeared in several specials and shows since then.

For example, Wilson appeared in the 2022 Cars miniseries Cars on the Road, which premiered on Disney+. He also reprised his role briefly in 2024s LEGO Pixar: BrickToons, in which he appeared in the episode Trust Yer Ol’ Pal, Mater. Wilson has lent his voice to a number of Cars video games, too, along with recording original lines for Cars Land at Disney California Adventure theme park.

2026 marks the twentieth anniversary of the Cars films, so it’s only fitting that Wilson will soon be joining the fold once again for Cars: Lightning Racers.

Owen Wilson is also set to appear in an untitled film from writer/director Nancy Myers, which is slated for release on Christmas Day in 2027. Wilson is one of many A-list actors to be cast in the film, which is currently in post-production, having completed principal photography earlier this year.

Along with Wilson, this untitled film also features Penélope Cruz, Kieran Culkin (a recent Academy Award winner), and Jude Law, although few details on his character have been revealed at this stage. Audiences can expect more information to be released about this film, including its title, at some point in 2027, thanks to its current expected release date.

#3468. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3467. The 7 Greatest Flintlock Fantasy Books of All Time, Ranked

Fantasy doesn't always have to revolve around castles, kingdoms, and sword-wielding knights. Flintlock fantasy takes the genre into a more technologically advanced era, inspired by the 17th, 18th, and early 19th centuries, when firearms were transforming warfare and political revolutions were reshaping entire societies.

These novels combine gunpowder weapons and industrial innovation with traditional fantasy elements such as sorcery and mythical creatures. Their worldbuilding tends to draw on the Age of Exploration, the Enlightenment, the American and French Revolutions, or the Napoleonic Wars, and the plots tend to have a military and political focus. These are the best books in the Flintlock subgenre, proving that it's a subgenre full of endless possibility.

"True change has never been bloodless." In this one, the first of a trilogy, we're transported to a society where the blood of dragons possesses extraordinary properties, allowing certain individuals known as the Blood-blessed to perform supernatural feats. These abilities have become essential to commerce and warfare, with powerful trading companies competing to control the increasingly scarce dragon blood supply. The blood is kind of like the spice in Dune, the way it warps culture and politics.

Against that backdrop, petty thief Claydon Torcreek is recruited for a dangerous expedition into unexplored territory, while highly skilled corporate agent Lizanne Lethridge undertakes an undercover mission, and Corrick Hilemore, the second lieutenant of an ironship, pursues brigands. Together, these characters give us an expansive understanding of its fictional world. That said, the action sequences are probably the highlight, combining espionage and naval combat, guns and blood magic.

"Can you be haunted by someone who isn't dead?" Django Wexler has written many solid fantasy books, including some for Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering. Ranking among the best of them, The Thousand Names is the opening entry in his Shadow Campaign series, which draws heavily from the Napoleonic era. It focuses on the soldiers of the Vordanai army stationed in a distant colonial territory. After a rebellion forces the surviving troops into retreat, the enigmatic Colonel Janus promises to transform their fortunes.

Among the soldiers serving under his command is Winter Ihernglass, a woman who has disguised herself as a man to escape her troubled past. Meanwhile, the ambitious officer Marcus d'Ivoire struggles to understand the increasingly unconventional strategies employed by his brilliant new commander. While the plot is juicy, the book ultimately stands out thanks to its unusually meticulous treatment of military organization and battle tactics.

"Doesn't matter how good your bullets are if you don't aim carefully." The Alloy of Law is set 300 years after author Brandon Sanderson's bestseller Mistborn, retaining that book's magic system (which involved "burning" certain metals for special powers) but surrounding it with a world inspired by the Wild West and the Industrial Revolution, all gun-slinging and train robberies. The main character is Waxillium Ladrian, a nobleman who has spent years working as a lawman in the frontier territories.

Following a personal tragedy, Wax returns to the bustling city of Elendel to assume responsibility for his family's declining fortunes, only to find himself up against a dangerous criminal organization. Fortunately, he's no pushover. Wax's unusual combination of powers allows him to manipulate metal and alter his weight. This means he can deflect incoming bullets, launch himself across rooftops, and alter the momentum of his own shots midair. Needless to say, his abilities make for some cool gunfights.

"The secret of gunpowder is that anyone—a man, a woman, a child, a cripple—can kill with it." Guns of the Dawn is a brutal standalone novel by author Adrian Tchaikovsky, perhaps best known for writing the masterful sci-fi novel Children of Time. It centers on Emily Marshwic, a young woman from a respectable family in the kingdom of Lascanne. When a devastating war against the neighboring nation of Denland breaks out, Emily is conscripted, forced to abandon her comfortable existence and confront the horrors of the frontline.

From here, the book nimbly fuses a Regency-era comedy of manners with gritty black-powder warfare, kind of like Jane Austen meets military fantasy. The tale takes us from drawing rooms and rolling estates to war-torn swamps ringing with the crack of muskets and the thud of artillery, the bite of a bayonet never far away.

"I am beginning to feel the need of a glass of wine to fortify myself against this conversation." This gem reinterprets the Napoleonic Wars by introducing dragons into the armies of Europe's competing empires. The plot follows William Laurence, a disciplined British naval captain whose life changes dramatically after his crew captures a French vessel carrying an extraordinarily valuable dragon egg. When the creature hatches, Laurence unexpectedly forms a bond with the young dragon, whom he names Temeraire.

This development forces him to abandon his promising naval career and join Britain's Aerial Corps, where dragons and their human crews play an essential role in defending the country against Napoleon. Adding dragons to any setting generally makes it more fun, but here author Naomi Novik's does so without sacrificing all that much historical authenticity. Indeed, the social conventions and military hierarchies of the era still feel real and well-researched.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

"Age is no guarantee of maturity." Promise of Blood is a combustible mix of adventure, revolution, elaborate magic systems, and hard-hitting gunpowder warfare. Kicking off the Powder Mage trilogy, it begins with Field Marshal Tamas orchestrating a bloody coup against the monarchy of Adro, overthrowing (and executing) the country's sorcerous elite. However, the revolution quickly creates new dangers, including political instability, foreign intervention, and even the possibility of divine retribution.

As Tamas attempts to consolidate his authority, his son Taniel, a talented powder mage, becomes involved in a deadly investigation, while retired investigator Adamat uncovers conspiracies threatening the fragile new government. The politics and intrigue are compelling, and the magic system is entertaining, too. Unlike traditional wizards, powder mages ingest or snort black powder to enter an addictive "powder trance" that grants superhuman strength and heightened senses, letting them extend rifle ranges far beyond normal limits and even curve bullets with their mind.

"Can a magician kill a man by magic?" Simply put, this is one of the greatest historical fantasy novels of all time, layering ancient supernatural traditions onto Regency-era England and the Napoleonic wars. Set in an alternative version of early 19th-century Britain, the story follows Gilbert Norrell, a reclusive scholar who astonishes English society by demonstrating that practical magic still exists. His accomplishments eventually attract the attention of Jonathan Strange, a younger and considerably more adventurous magician who becomes Norrell's pupil.

Eventually, their contrasting philosophies metastasize into a bitter rivalry, particularly concerning the dangerous and mysterious legacy of England's forgotten magical traditions. Writer Susanna Clarke grounds all these fantastical elements in an immersive world, richly recreating the period's social conventions. She even borrows from the prose style of the era's classic writers such as Jane Austen and Charles Dickens. Talk about ambitious.

#3466. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3464. Slow Horses officially moves beyond the books with 2 more seasons

Seems like Jack Lowden isn’t going to be James Bond

In an interview with The Times ahead of the UK release of Anton Corbijn’s thriller A Talent for Murder, star Olivia Cooke spoke about her role on Apple TV’s hit spy show Slow Horses. Cooke said that shooting had begun for the series’ eighth season, which would be its last, and that she was so depressed by the news she was crying in her makeup chair. “We’re all melancholy, distracted,” she said. It turns out there’s no reason for tears.

Apple announced today that Slow Horses has been renewed for two more seasons. Season 6 ended in October, and production has already been completed for season 7, which is expected to be released in fall 2027. The series keeps to an exceptionally tight production schedule – the writers’ room for season 7 opened while season 6 was still being filmed. That’s allowed Apple to be extremely consistent with the release schedule, dropping at least one six-episode season annually since the show premiered in 2022.

Cooke’s report seemed believable because Slow Horses is running out of material. The series is a faithful adaptation of Mick Herron’s bestselling Slough House series, with each season typically corresponding to a single novel. Season 6 compressed Herron’s sixth and seventh books, Joe Country and Slough House. Season 7 will adapt Herron’s 2022 book, Bad Actors, and season 8 will adapt his 2025 book, Clown Town. Herron hasn’t said that he’s finished with the series, but given how far ahead Apple works, it is going to run out of material unless the author delivers a new book soon.

Without Herron’s tightly written John le Carré-style spy stories to provide the plot, further seasons of Slow Horses could decline in quality. The risk seems especially high given that series creator and showrunner Will Smith left Slow Horses after season 5. Slow Horses is one of the best shows on TV, so hopefully there’s a good plan in place for further adventures of the misanthropic spymaster Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) and his squad of failed MI5 agents. I would hate to see the series fall apart like Game of Thrones did when showrunners David Benioff and D. B. Weiss moved past what George R.R. Martin had written.

Cooke revealing that she’s on set for season 8 is a bit of a spoiler given how season 6 ended with her character Sid Baker fleeing MI5 custody. River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) went to find Sid, and was seemingly poisoned. Assuming the show continues to closely follow the plot of the books, neither River nor Sid will be part of the main cast of season 7, but they will return for season 8. That means Slow Horses’ renewal probably came with a bit of professional bad news for Lowden.

River thinks he’s James Bond even though he’s just as much a screw-up as the rest of his colleagues. Ironically, Lowden is considered a frontrunner for the upcoming Bond movie directed by Denis Villeneuve. Other lead contenders include Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, Nicholas Hoult, and Robert Pattinson. While it’s possible that Slow Horses will actually kill River off and leave Lowden free to join the Bond franchise, it seems more likely that Villeneuve is going with another actor and River will just keep irritating Lamb for years to come.

#3463. 6 Horror Series Better Than American Horror Story

From TV powerhouse Ryan Murphy, American Horror Story's first season, Murder House, drew immediate attention with its all-star cast that included Connie Britton, Dylan McDermott, Jennifer Lange, Sarah Paulson, and Frances Conroy. Even more importantly, Murder House was genuinely compelling, balancing horror, drama, and emotional depth in one self-contained season.

At the time, a horror anthology felt both unique and timeless, evoking nostalgia for series like The Twilight Zone while still delivering something modern and fresh. For the next several years, American Horror Story continued to successfully reinvent itself, attracting stars like Lady Gaga, Kathy Bates, and Angela Bassett, and making new ones out of the likes of Evan Peters and Emma Roberts.

In its prime, the anthology format seemed to promise that American Horror Story could live forever. Eventually, though, the show began to feel like a caricature of itself, relying on the allure of fan-favorite actors and buzzy pieces of stunt casting. The show's horror became more campy and less genuinely scary, and new stories increasingly connected to previous ones in attempts to recapture the original magic.

This reached an unprecedented level in the show's most recent season, 13, which was a massive crossover of American Horror Story's first five seasons, as well as Cult and Apocalypse​​​. The thinnest of storylines connected the ambitious mashup, and even as fan-favorite actors reprised their most iconic roles, 13 felt like it forgot the show's own plot, making it a shell of what American Horror Story once was.

Though American Horror Story was once a pillar of the horror television landscape, these six shows have far surpassed the example it set.

Today, Mike Flanagan is the king of horror television. With hits ranging from the original Midnight Mass to the latest adaptation of Stephen King's Carrie, the writer and showrunner has proven that he is far from a one-hit wonder when it comes to telling scary stories on TV. His very first TV projects, though, felt truly like an elevated American Horror Story.

The Haunting of Hill House, inspired by Shirley Jackson's novel of the same name, was an immediate hit that put Netflix on the map for its horror limited series. Both terrifying and emotionally poignant, Hill House took extensive creative liberties from its source material to tell a story that felt simultaneously gothic and contemporary.

The same could be said of Flanagan's next limited series, The Haunting of Bly Manor. While Bly Manor was technically its own, separate show, it shared a title format, theme music, and tagline ("You're expected") with Hill House, setting the stage for a Haunting of... anthology of modernized adaptations of gothic horror literature.

Like Hill House, Bly Manor took a character-first approach without losing the genuine chills of a ghost story. In the end, Bly Manor proved to be truly haunting in every sense of the word, making the two projects the gold standard of contemporary self-contained horror.

Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen was Netflix's first major horror limited series made in the wake of Mike Flanagan's migration to Prime Video. The limited series, produced by the Duffer Brothers, proved that the streamer was capable of maintaining the high expectations of quality set by Flanagan's works.

The creepy story of Jerry Poole and Coldies Frozen Custard plays a more important role in Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen than you may think.

At first, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen relied primarily on its unsettling tone as Rachel (Camila Morrone) prepared for her wedding with a gut feeling that something wasn't right. As it went on, though, the show became a rich, intertwined story of love, family dysfunction, and tall tales coming to life.

Morrone's down-to-earth and utterly likable performance set the groundwork for her character's intuition to be taken seriously, while Jennifer Jason Leigh and Adam DiMarco rounded out the cast with similarly compelling performances. In the end, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen delivered on the promise of its title in a way that felt earned and full of equal doses of heartache and horror.

Netflix's latest record-breaking acquired series deserves its place in the streamer's Top 10. Set in a quaint yet terrifying, inescapable town, From is among the most memorable folk horror series made in recent years. Complete with flesh-eating nocturnal monsters, time travel, and an ancient, shapeshifting trickster seemingly behind it all, From utilizes classic horror imagery in a completely new way.

While its strange premise and laundry list of unsolved mysteries have led to frequent comparisons to Lost, From is definitively scarier, giving just as much attention to the genuine terror that faces the townspeople as the overarching mystery of why they've been brought there in the first place.

While the vampire-adjacent monsters offer ample nightmare fuel in and of themselves, From also taps into a more psychological horror with the promise that if the townspeople were to fail to solve the show's mystery, their demise would be at their own hands. Throughout the series, the Township has worked to drain its residents of hope and instead sow the seeds of division and violence among them.

Bates Motel served as a prequel to Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho, yet it was set in the present day. The temporal disconnect gave the show an odd, off-kilter feel from the very start, and Bates Motel continued to keep viewers on their toes despite the conclusion promised by the 1960 movie.

Vera Farmiga, Nestor Carbonell, and Olivia Cooke all delivered memorable performances that greatly expanded the world created in Psycho, but the true standout was Freddie Highmore's work as Norman Bates. Highmore's Norman was complex, multifaceted, and equal parts endearing and dangerous.

His descent to the state the character is seen in Psycho was a slow burn of impressive proportions, and the subtlety of his mannerisms and behavior created a believable confusion around Norman's state of mind. Though it ran for five successful seasons, Bates Motel deserves a lasting legacy within the horror genre.

Its vampire-centric premise makes True Blood immediately brings American Horror Story's Coven​​​​​​ to mind, but comparing the two actually cements how much more gritty, grounding, and emotionally resonant HBO's 2007 series really was.

With a plot involving vampires, werewolves, shapeshifters, fairies, and witches, True Blood's premise was high fantasy to the extreme, yet in execution, the show was actually a powerful character study and cultural exploration of the American South. Even while dating vampires and werewolves, Anna Paquin's Sookie Stackhouse was, first and foremost, a resilient, likable, and completely believable Louisiana girl.

Paquin's performance gave True Blood its down-to-earth tone, but the show also broadened its scope as it explored themes of religious prejudice, queerness in the South, and female independence. True Blood was often silly, but it also created a serious and genuine world that felt like it could, somehow, exist within our own.

Arguably the biggest breakout series of 2026, Widow's Bay has offered an entirely new take on the horror-comedy genre mashup. Rather than watering down its scares with jokes, Widow's Bay​​​​​'s first season was both laugh-out-loud funny and genuinely eerie.

The cursed town of Widow's Bay poses a very real threat to its residents, yet the depiction of how those residents respond to that threat takes a tone akin to a workplace comedy. Matthew Rhys' self-proclaimed first major foray into comedy is a phenomenal acting feat as he imbues the bumbling Mayor Tom Loftis with pitch-perfect line delivery and a heartfelt, if not misguided, passion for bettering the town.

Widow's Bay's season 1 finale raised the stakes on both a plot and character level, setting the stage for the show's sophomore season to be just as much of an event as its first. All in all, Widow's Bay is a testament to the limitless potential the horror genre holds today.

#3462. Netflix’s Major Crime Franchise Starter Officially Becomes a Streaming Juggernaut

The crime genre is a staple of television. Some of the most popular shows of all time include crime elements, from The Sopranos to Breaking Bad to Law & Order. The enduring appeal of the crime genre lies in its ability to explore the darkest corners of human nature while maintaining high stakes. Whether following the ruthless rise of a cartel boss or the methodical work of homicide detectives, viewers are drawn to the moral ambiguity and tension inherent in breaking the law. Television allows you to root for bad and dangerous people without having any skin in the game. It can also allow you to hate them as much as you want to the point of wishing some characters would meet an untimely end.

12 years ago, Starz aired one of the most popular crime shows in the world. Titled Power, the series was created by Courtney A. Kemp and executive produced by Curtis "50 Cent" Jackson. The crime thriller focuses on James "Ghost" St. Patrick, a New York drug kingpin trying to escape the game through his upscale nightclub, Truth. However, it is easier said than done, as he is caught up between the ruthless drug game, a failing marriage, law enforcement, and the resurfacing of the love of his life. Power delivered six exhilarating seasons full of excellent performances, good music, and jaw-dropping twists. And recently, all seasons just landed on Netflix.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

As the mothership courts more viewers, the universe is set to continue with two more shows. Power: Origins turns back the clock to late 20th-century New York as Ghost and his friend Tommy rise in the game. #3461. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers
